title: Chainsaw maker STIHL's chief calls for longer hours without extra pay
description: In an opinion piece for Euronews, Dr Nikolas Stihl, chairman of world-leading chainsaw maker STIHL, calls for reforms including a 40-hour working week without extra pay to safeguard Germany's prosperity and welfare state.
fullText:
The family entrepreneur from Waiblingen in southern Germany does not mince his words: "The German economy has been stuck in crisis mode for years. The prerequisite for overcoming the persistent weakness in growth is better framework conditions," Stihl said.

In 2025, STIHL generated €5.48 billion in revenue and employed 20,246 people worldwide. Founded by Andreas Stihl in 1926, the company is celebrating its 100th anniversary. Nikolas Stihl is the founder's grandson.

Family businessman Stihl takes a long-term view, and for him one thing is clear: "The situation of the German economy is serious, very serious. In the past eight years we have lost around 15 percent of our industrial output. Month after month Germany is losing around 15,000 industrial jobs."

The industrial base, he warns, is at risk of eroding – and with it prosperity and the welfare state. According to the company, STIHL has been the world's best-selling chainsaw brand since 1971. Nikolas Stihl acknowledges that "the US tariffs, China's aggressive industrial policy and geopolitical tensions" are also weighing on companies like his. But he argues that it is mainly home-grown problems holding firms back: "an overregulated economy, high energy costs, high labour costs, high taxes and a declining level of education and qualifications."

The federal government’s planned reforms – covering statutory health insurance, pensions, taxes and the labour market – are good compromises, but they do not go far enough to pull Germany out of its structural crisis. If these compromises were now to be "unpicked", it would have devastating consequences for business confidence in politics, the entrepreneur warns.

Stihl says: "Now we need to muster all our strength for further reforms that will then generate tangible investment and growth impulses. For that, the governing coalition and the social partners must overcome their own reservations in order to live up to their responsibility towards Germany."

The next steps, he argues, should include cutting red tape, increasing the overall volume of work in the economy, reducing labour costs and creating additional incentives for research and development.

Stihl is calling for "high-quality public administration" with clear rules, streamlined and swift procedures, reasonable reporting requirements, and processes that are digital and supported by AI. "Accordingly, statutory reporting requirements should generally be abolished and retained only where their necessity is explicitly justified. If public authorities act much more as service providers for citizens and companies, that increases trust in Germany as a business location and in politics."

For Stihl, the key issue is increasing the volume of work – in other words, Germans need to work more again: "If we want to maintain our prosperity and keep social benefits at a high level, the total volume of work in the economy has to increase. A higher volume of work boosts economic output. In that sense, the debate about more work is a debate about preserving our prosperity, and by no means a debate about employees being lazy."

Germany must use every available option to increase the volume of work: by incentivising overtime, extending working lives with fair exceptions for physically demanding jobs, making better use of the existing labour pool – including unemployed and part-time workers – and attracting skilled workers from abroad.

Stihl also calls for sick pay to be paid only from the second day of sickness and for phone-in sick notes to be abolished. Productivity gains from digitalisation and the growing use of AI will not offset the negative effects of demographic change.

From October 2026, collective bargaining talks in the metalworking and electrical industries are due to begin between trade unions and employers. Stihl warns: "We no longer have the productivity advantage over key competitors that used to justify our high labour costs. That is why I advocate increasing weekly working hours to 40, without any pay compensation.

He acknowledges that he is asking a great deal of employees, but says he does not want to take anything away from anyone.

The aim, he insists, is to remain competitive, keep production in Germany and safeguard jobs. STIHL has production companies in eight countries, as well as 40 of its own sales and marketing subsidiaries and more than 50,000 specialist dealers worldwide.

When it comes to non-wage labour costs – including contributions to pension, health, long-term care and unemployment insurance – he says a ceiling of 40% of gross wages is the maximum that can be accepted.

Stihl is also calling for more attractive conditions for innovative companies, including regulatory breathing space, greater tax incentives and wider access to venture capital. "Overall, innovation and the granting of approvals must be given an even higher priority than at present and must not be held back by bureaucracy."

Future-focused fields such as the industrial use of artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, medical technology, space travel and quantum technologies should receive more targeted support.

The conclusion reached by the head of the world's leading chainsaw brand and a global technology company is clear: "We must not waste any more time, because only a high-performance and competitive business location can secure prosperity and a strong welfare state. Germany has proved many times that it can reinvent itself."

For the public to embrace the challenges ahead, "a ruthless stocktake of the current situation" is needed, followed by an overall plan setting out the changes people can expect. "The time has come to act with determination," says Nikolas Stihl.

title: Erin Piacenti, killed in Times Square stabbing, was a 'superstar' at Bank of America known for mentoring junior teammates
description: Erin Piacenti only spent 18 months at Bank of America before she was killed, but colleagues said she made an outsize impact with her mentorship.
fullText:
Erin Piacenti, who was killed in Times Square on Monday, was known as a mentor at Bank of America.

Colleagues remembered her not only for her sharp legal mind, but love of books, Disney, and family.

Piacenti's boss remembers describing her as a 'superstar' to senior management before her death.

When Erin Piacenti walked into Bank of America on Monday after five months on maternity leave, she found pink daisies sitting on her desk. Welcome signs were strung around the office she shared with a few teammates. Piacenti showed them photos of Madison, her newborn daughter, before settling in to read case law.

That afternoon, Piacenti was fatally stabbed in Times Square in what police described as an unprovoked attack. She was 32.

Though Piacenti only started as a vice president in the firm's Americas Business Selection and Conflicts group around 18 months ago, she'd already made an impact on the small team. Hallie Ziesmer, the head of the roughly 20-person group, described Piacenti as a "superstar" in conversations with senior management before her death, and remembers interviewing Piacenti at the end of 2024.

"It was probably one of the shortest interviews, because I think within three minutes I wanted to hire her," Ziesmer, who was Piacenti's direct boss, said on Friday. "She was obviously very intelligent, very capable. She was polished but down-to-earth."

Piacenti was attacked by Pamela Cisneros, 49, who also injured another victim before officers shot her and killed her at the scene.

There's been a wave of support on and beyond Wall Street since the event, and a GoFundMe to help her daughter has raised more than $800,000. Many Bank of America employees have contributed, a spokesperson for the bank said.

Before joining Bank of America, Piacenti worked at the law firm Davis Polk for more than three years, focusing on mergers and acquisitions for part of that time. She started her career as a buyer at Bloomingdale's and graduated magna cum laude from Fordham Law. Piacenti had a niche focus at the bank, helping investment bankers prepare disclosure documents for companies gearing up for an M&A transaction and clients navigate a thicket of regulations. A colleague remembers her as resourceful, always finding creative solutions on her own.

Piacenti would mentor more junior teammates who didn't have the same legal expertise, Ziesmer said. Many of them have spent time in Ziesmer's office this week, remembering how detailed and caring Piacenti was with her help. One junior employee who sat across from Piacenti said in an email that she reviewed much of their work, and had offered personal advice on top of professional tips during their occasional coffees.

"She could have, on some days, left the office to be home, but she would spend time with juniors. She wanted them to understand and share a passion for what she was doing. She really enjoyed it," Ziesmer said.

Piacenti would often talk about visiting her four younger siblings, or books, or Disney. When the team attended a cooking class last year, the same colleague who admired Piacenti's resourcefulness said she made the best dish (and helped save them, an inadequate chef). When another colleague ran into her on the Q train one morning, she was thrilled to introduce them to her husband, Frank, whom she talked about all the time.

Around the holidays, Piacenti brought dozens of cookies into the office after she and Frank hosted the family's Christmas cookie party at their new home in New Jersey.

Ziesmer says the team now plans to bring in cookies every year.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Iran claims a strike on a US ship in the Strait of Hormuz but the US denies it
description: Iran said Sunday it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, a claim that the U.S. military dismissed as a “total lie.
fullText:
CAIRO (AP) — Iran said Sunday it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, a claim that the U.S. military dismissed as a "total lie."

The purported attack came a day after the U.S. military said forces struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to Navy warships being targeted with ballistic missiles. Experts called it a dangerous escalation after Iran's previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping.

The war began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. But since a fragile ceasefire agreement was announced in June, on-and-off fighting has persisted, with both sides trying to inflict military and economic pain as negotiations have collapsed.

The United States and Iran resumed attacks last week, following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz and areas along Iran's southern coast again being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a U.S. bombardment that returned attention to the area where a school was hit in the war's opening strikes.

The Trump administration appears to have adopted a dual-prong approach to the conflict, responding militarily to attacks on the strait while going after foreign financial institutions that handle Iran's money.

But Tehran's hard-line new senior leaders have signaled a willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions. Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions, and now a U.S. blockade of its ports, and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil.

Tehran's new leverage focuses on the Strait of Hormuz that is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments. It was seen as an international waterway before the war began.

On Sunday, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that on average, 9 million barrels of oil a day are getting through the strait, which should help to relieve pressure on energy prices. His estimate appeared to exceed average flows over the past 28 days through the strait, according to TankerTrackers.com and other sources.

Wright told CNN that with oil also flowing through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows."

But those flows depend on the presence of the U.S. Navy to help escort tankers and provide some protection against possible Iranian attack. Wright said he expected that other countries would eventually support the Navy's efforts.

Meanwhile, Iran's nuclear program, the issue that contributed to the outbreak of the war, was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June.

Diplomats say the U.S., Britain, France and Germany now seek to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations.

Magdy reported from Cairo and Frankel reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington and Josh Boak in Bridgewater, New Jersey, contributed to this report.

title: The skull of a saint that was discovered during renovations
description: Ambrose Barlow was found guilty of treason and sentenced to death in 1641.
fullText:
On 25 April 1641, Ambrose Barlow celebrated a secret Easter Sunday mass at Morleys Hall near Astley in Greater Manchester.

But, by the end of the service, the building had been surrounded by a 400-strong armed group led by a local vicar.

"King Charles I issued a decree stating that all Catholic priests must leave within a month...and if they didn't, they would face the consequences of treason," said the Right Reverend John Arnold, the Bishop of Salford.

King Charles I wanted to prove that he supported the Protestant faith while keeping his political enemies at bay as parliament were suspicious of his Catholic wife.

The congregation urged Ambrose Barlow to hide but Arnold said he refused and instead ordered the doors to be opened and surrendered peacefully.

"He didn't make any attempt to avoid arrest," said Arnold.

"He was really concerned for the safety of the people attending mass - about 150 of them."

He was taken to Lancaster Castle where he was imprisoned.

After four months, he was put on trial, charged with being a priest.

He was found guilty of treason and sentenced to death.

"On 10 September, which is now his feast day, he was hung, drawn, and quartered," said Arnold.

"And his skull was put on a pike as a demonstration to people that this is what happens if you are a Catholic."

It was a warning to all who refused to conform to the state religion.

The Catholic priest is the subject of a new episode of Hidden Manchester on BBC Sounds.

The skull of St Ambrose Barlow is a sacred relic, which is kept at Wardley Hall in Worsley on red velvet inside a locked, glass-fronted cabinet recessed into a wall on the main staircase.

Arnold said the skull was retrieved and brought to Wardley Hall, which has been the residence of the Bishop of Salford since 1930.

"At that stage Wardley Hall belonged to the Downes family who were the cousins to the Barlow family," said Arnold, who resides at Wardley Hall.

"Francis Downes placed the skull in a casket in the wall of the then chapel in Wardley Hall."

The skull was accidentally discovered by Matthew Moreton during renovation work in 1745.

Later forensic tests in the 20th century confirmed it was the skull of Ambrose Barlow.

On 25 October 1970, Pope Paul VI officially canonised 40 martyrs of England and Wales in a ceremony at St Peter's Basilica in Rome.

This honoured Catholic men and women killed in the 16th and 17th centuries for their beliefs.

Ambrose Barlow became Saint Ambrose Barlow.

The skull of St Ambrose Barlow remains at Wardley Hall where private groups can see it by appointment.

Arnold said it was unusual to have such a relic in a private collection.

"It's rare for it to be in a private house, but Catholics have long had a tradition of relics, either pieces of a body of a saint or a possession of a saint," he said.

"It's a way people have found of coming closer to the reality of the holiness of the person."

title: Ancient cave art discovery suggests first known humans in Ireland walked over from Wales
description: During the most recent Ice Age, researchers believe there was a "lost land bridge" between Wales and Ireland.
fullText:
Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discovery of ancient cave art.

During the most recent Ice Age, when much of the British Isles were beneath a vast continental glacier, the depleted sea levels opened a "lost land bridge" between modern-day Pembrokeshire and the south-east tip of Ireland, around Rosslare.

According to rock expert Dr George Nash, from Liverpool University, the opportunities presented by this pathway would have been too good for hunter gatherers to ignore.

Now, alongside an international team of experts, Nash has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000 years ago, around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

Nash, who coordinated the Lost Land Bridge Project, said there would have been a forested and grassland plateau around 46 miles (76 km) coast-to-coast.

With summertime temperatures typically -10°C to -20°C, Nash said the pathway would have supported wild horses, mammoth, bison, reindeer and other large herbivores, which fed off the hardy sedges, mosses and lichens growing through the fertile, but near-frozen soil.

Nash said he had always believed - from what he had gleaned throughout his career about human movement during the period - that it was inconceivable that people would not have utilised the opportunity the pathway presented.

This led him to assemble his multi-disciplinary team of experts from University College Dublin and the University of Adelaide, along with academics from Dubai, Wales and Portugal.

"Up until now the earliest evidence archaeologists had found - through accidental discovery - was from around 10,500 years ago, but everyone - not just me - knew that simply couldn't have been correct.

"We just weren't looking hard enough, and not in the right places. The principle we worked on was 'absence of proof isn't proof of absence'."

He said advances in artificial intelligence (AI) had been a game-changer.

"With the help of caving specialist Shane Diffily and digital mapping consultant Darren Lee, we were able to fill a computer algorithm with everything we knew about the characteristics of cave dwellings in south Wales and set it to work searching for similar sites in Ireland, without us trudging blindly around the countryside, hoping to bump into something which looked promising."

What their computer model spat out was 28 potential caves in south-west Ireland which the team investigated.

Eight of them were found to have cave art which they believe dates from at least 15,000 years ago and possibly much earlier, and around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

The team are currently unwilling to be more precise about the location of the caves, for fear that they may be vandalised or looted.

"We know that modern day south Wales was settled from around 35,000 to 40,000 years ago, by intrepid early modern humans from southern England, France and Spain, crossing the then dried-up land bridges of the English and Bristol Channels - seasonally settling in caves along the inhabitable strip of land stretching from Chepstow to St Davids," said Nash.

"Over 20,000 years their art progressed from primitive line drawings which may have been early tally charts, to more figurative and representative depictions of the world around them, and what we've found in Ireland is yet another progression from that."

The rock art which the Lost Land Bridge Project has uncovered includes engravings on the cave walls, paintings in ochre and charcoal and line sketches indented into clay and earth by fingertips.

Nash believes the growing population put pressure on humans to move ever more west and northwards.

"There were around 100 human-inhabited caves on The Gower Peninsula for example, in a time when the technology didn't yet exist for human groups to create their own free-standing dwellings.

"The ambient temperature within these caves would have remained between 10°C and 15°C all year round, so with bearskin covers and fires at the entrance - which also helped to ward-off predators - it would have been quite a cosy place to live, especially compared with the -20°C outside.

"Competition for these caves would have been intense.

"As family networks grew, knowledge of how to survive by following animal migration routes improved and they must have become bolder."

The Lost Land Bridge Project team believe the potential for more future discoveries is high.

"The sites we've currently explored are in south-west Ireland, but it's illogical to presume that early humans just bypassed Wexford, Waterford and Cork, and ploughed on west," said Nash.

"There must be more, and even earlier places which are just waiting for us to find them. This project is now pushing the boundaries of what we consider to be the final vestiges of a north-west European frontier. It's all very exciting."

title: Trump's approval drops among Republicans ahead of midterms, new poll shows
description: NBC News unveiled new polling that shows a drop in approval for President Donald Trump among Republicans.
fullText:
President Donald Trump's support among Republican voters dropped in a new poll less than two months from November's crucial midterm elections.

An NBC News Decision Desk survey conducted from Aug. 20 to Sept. 1 found a near 10 percentage point drop among Republicans who say they "strongly approve" of the president's job performance. In polling conducted in March and April, 52% of Republicans said they strongly approved of the president's performance, compared to 31% who said they somewhat approve. Now, 41% of Republicans said they strongly approve, and those who somewhat approve have jumped to 39%.

The results, unveiled by the network's star data expert Steve Kornacki, found that Trump's overall approval rating landed at 36% – marking a record NBC polling low this term. That's also close to a low of 33% in a Reuters poll released last month.

The polling comes as Americans brace for the final quarter of the year amid economic fears and growing uncertainty about the Iran war.

First-ever GOP midterm convention is this week. Here's how to watch

Trump has said he's optimistic about his party's midterm performance − despite longstanding precedent suggesting that the party with presidential power typically loses seats in both the House and Senate.

"For some reason, the voters tend to go the other way. I think we're gonna do very well," Trump said during an Aug. 30 appearance on Fox News' "Sunday Night In America With Trey Gowdy."

Trump and Vice President JD Vance next week are expected to address the first GOP midterm convention in recent history. The pair will seek to galvanize voters in Dallas before the party goes on defense in major swing states before Election Day.

The NBC News polling surveyed 7,105 adults online from Aug. 20 to Sept. 1. It has a margin of error of +/- 3.3 percentage points.

Contributing: Kinsey Crowley, Fernando Cervantes Jr.

title: Five European nations seek deals to send migrants out of the EU
description: (Refiles to remove extraneous reporting credit)  COPENHAGEN, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Five European nations aim to sign deals this year to send migrants without legal residency ‌to countries outside the Eur...
fullText:
(Refiles to remove extraneous reporting credit)

COPENHAGEN, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Five European nations aim to sign deals this year to send migrants without legal residency ‌to countries outside the European Union, they said at a meeting hosted by Denmark on ‌Friday.

Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said they had agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with a non-European ​Union country on return facilities, the latest effort by European nations to reduce immigration.

The countries, known as the Group of Five, did not name the nations they expect to host return centres.

"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year that will enable the establishment of return hubs," German Interior Minister Alexander ‌Dobrindt told reporters at a press ⁠conference in Copenhagen.

The group, which has held a series of meetings this year, plans to reconvene in Munich, Germany, at the end of September.

The European Parliament ⁠in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to set up centres abroad, in what critics say could weaken safeguards for asylum seekers.

The Council of Europe, ​a ​non-EU body that promotes human rights, democracy and the ​rule of law across the continent, in ‌July said return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks", and several other groups have also criticised the plan.

Danish Refugee Council Secretary General Charlotte Slente said it would be better to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which focuses on stricter border screening, faster asylum and return procedures, and expanded digital systems for managing asylum claims.

"Return hubs focus on a small number of returns, they will not stop people ‌from taking even more dangerous routes, and they could ​violate basic human rights," Slente said.

Denmark expects to be ready ​to send migrants to the return hub by ​the end of 2027, Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov said.

"It's a new ‌chance to have a life in a ​partner country," he said, adding ​that the five nations would be in dialogue with the UN body, the International Organization for Migration, and the UN Refugee Agency for their next steps.

A UNHCR spokesperson said the agency ​had not been approached with details ‌of a proposal and could not comment on the arrangements being discussed.

title: Nepali woman found alive days after family began mourning rites
description: Believing she had perished in Nepal's deadly floods, the family of Chandika Kumari Shrestha started the ritual of mourning the elderly woman's death
fullText:
BETRAWATI, Nepal, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Believing she had perished in Nepal's deadly floods, the family of Chandika Kumari Shrestha started the ritual of mourning the elderly woman's death.

Ten ‌days later, rescuers found her alive inside her collapsed home in the devastated Betrawati village, ‌where she had survived in a narrow pocket of air amid water and mud.

"The four-storey house was swept (away) by the floods and ​the house was left in the middle of a quicksand. While walking around it, we heard a voice 'save me,'" police officer Mahendra Darnal said.

In a rescue operation on Saturday lasting 45 minutes, Darnal and his team found Shrestha in a confined space and sent her to an army hospital.

"I was in touch with the family and ‌they had started the 11-day mourning ⁠period," Darnal said.

Shrestha was among the hundreds missing in Betrawati, an area among the hardest hit by the floods in Nepal and engulfed with white deposits compacted almost ⁠like concrete. Crews continue to recover scores of dead bodies.

The town's market and most residential buildings, some as tall as four storeys, were almost completely buried under debris left by a torrent that swept through the valley, part ​of a ​disaster that killed more than 1,300 people across Nepal. ​Thousands remain unaccounted for.

Rescue workers wearing hard ‌hats were seen digging with shovels, while some were crawling through the gaps of collapsed buildings periodically blowing whistles to get the attention of anyone trapped and alive.

Five days earlier, 24 bodies were found in a decomposed state in Betrawati's market area in a building that had contained a small shop, Darnal said.

Eleven days since a glacial collapse triggered the devastating floods, close to 5,000 are still ‌missing.

Hundreds of bodies have been swept onto the banks of ​rivers far from the ravaged Rasuwa district. In Chitwan, hundreds of ​miles away, several rounds of mass burials ​have taken place for unidentified and badly decomposed bodies.

Even as hope is beginning to ‌fade, Nepal authorities continue their effort to ​look for people stuck in ​tunnels and under the thick deposits of mud that have hardened over buildings.

Since Friday, they have pulled out three people from the tunnels, including a Chinese citizen by the Trishuli river, where ​more than 900 are believed to ‌be trapped.

Others like Shrestha have survived in extraordinary conditions, including an 8-year-old boy who was ​also reunited with his mother.

title: Two killed as car hits group of cyclists
description: Three people have been arrested in connection to the incident near Gravesend.
fullText:

Two of the cyclists - a man in his 60s and woman in her 50s - were confirmed dead by emergency services on the scene, the force added.

Their next of kin have been informed.

A third cyclist was taken to a local hospital for treatment with minor injuries, according to officers.

Two men aged 20 and 21 were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

A 19-year-old woman was also detained on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Kent Police said the road was closed while an investigation took place.

The force is now appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident or saw the car or cyclists before the crash to contact them.

title: Machete-wielding MS-13 gangster wanted for murder walks free after Biden-appointed judge releases him: DHS
description: A convicted MS-13 killer known as "La Bruja" or "the witch" is free in California after a federal judge ruled ICE held him without a required bond hearing for five months.
fullText:
An MS-13 gang member convicted in a savage execution-style murder is out of federal custody in California after a federal judge ordered his immediate release, igniting fury from the Trump administration.

U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta ordered the release of David Antonio Aviles Perez, 35, aka "the witch," after finding that immigration officials held him for five months without giving him a bond hearing or determining whether he posed a danger to the public or a flight risk.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin accused the Biden-appointed judge of putting the public in danger by ordering Aviles Perez's release.

Dhs Eviscerates Media For 'Absolute Absurdity' Over Concern About 'Worst Of The Worst' Activist Judges List

"This radical activist judge has put American lives at risk by releasing a wanted murderer," Mullin said in a statement Saturday.

"This is now the SECOND time this dangerous illegal has been released back onto the streets in California," he added. "Because sanctuary politicians want to play politics from the bench, innocent Americans are in danger."

Sanctuary Laws Could Stop Police From Protecting Kids. So We're Suing California

The case centers on a brutal 2014 gang killing in El Salvador and a legal fight over the Trump administration's authority to detain immigrants while removal proceedings unfold.

Alvise Perez, identified by Salvadoran prosecutors as an active MS-13 member also known as "La Bruja," or "The Witch," was convicted while outside El Salvador in December 2025 and sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated murder.

Ice Nabs Accused Ms-13 Killer Hiding In Northern Virginia Suburb

Prosecutors said Aviles Perez and another MS-13 member chased a man through a mountainous area in La Unión before fellow gang members forced the victim to stop and kneel.

The victim was held by the shoulders as Aviles Perez and his accomplice approached, prosecutors said.

The gang members then shot the man in the chest, back and face before fleeing. Both defendants were tried and convicted while outside the country.

Aviles Perez entered the U.S. at an unknown date and location, according to DHS.

Illegal Immigrant Charged With Brutal Slaying One Day After California Judge Released Him: Dhs

He was arrested in Monterey, California, in 2023, after allegedly swinging a machete at a homeless man at Laguna Grande Park near Monterey State Beach. He allegedly hid the weapon before officers recovered it from a nearby Holiday Inn parking lot.

Aviles Perez was charged and convicted after the incident but later released from custody. DHS blamed California's sanctuary policies, which limit cooperation between local authorities and federal immigration officials.

Dhs Buys Two California Migrant Detention Centers For $1.5B To Boost Ice Deportation Capacity

ICE agents arrested him again in San Diego on March 26 and took him into custody pending his removal to El Salvador.

He was held at the Otay Mesa Detention Center pending removal to El Salvador until Ohta ordered his immediate release Aug. 26, federal court records show.

After nearly five months in immigration custody, Aviles Perez filed a petition challenging his detention and seeking his immediate release.

Ohta ruled that immigration officials violated his Fifth Amendment due process rights by holding him without an individualized assessment of whether he was dangerous or likely to flee.

"Although Petitioner appears to have previously been convicted following a fight with another individual in May 2023, the government has offered no evidence that it detained him after considering those facts and making an individualized determination of his danger to the public or flight risk," Ohta wrote.

Federal Judge In New York Ties Trump Admin Hands On Arrests At Immigration Courts

The judge said federal officials gave Aviles Perez "no process before or after his detention" and had not shown that providing a hearing would place an undue burden on the government.

Ohta ordered his immediate release and barred ICE from detaining him again unless an immigration judge first holds a bond hearing and determines that renewed detention is warranted.

A status report was filed in the case Aug. 27, one day after the release order. DHS said Aviles Perez was subsequently released from federal custody.

The ruling did not clear Aviles Perez of wrongdoing or find that he posed no danger. It focused on whether immigration officials followed the required process to justify keeping him detained.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom appointed Ohta to the San Diego County Superior Court in December 2020, according to the governor's office.

Biden Judge Torches Trump Ice Crackdown As 'Devoid Of Rational Explanation,' Nukes Courthouse Arrest Policy

President Joe Biden nominated her to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California in September 2021. The Senate confirmed her that December, and her judicial commission was issued later that month, according to the Federal Judicial Center.

Mullin vowed that the ruling would not derail the administration's immigration crackdown.

"DHS and ICE will not be deterred by these partisan games," he said. "If California's leaders won't protect Americans, DHS will."

Fox News Digital reached out to Ohta's office for additional comment and confirmation surrounding Aviles Perez's release.

title: Born here but deported. A Texas man's harrowing ordeal.
description: A traffic stop in Texas landed Brian Morales García, a U.S. citizen, in immigration custody. After he was deported to Mexico, a lawsuit helped bring him back.
fullText:
Brian José Morales García was riding beside his boss through the Texas Hill Country, bound for an air-conditioning job near Fredericksburg, when a state trooper stopped their pickup truck.

Over the next four days, the 25-year-old was shuttled through a succession of detention facilities. Along the way, his attorney said, he was stripped, shoved and threatened with years in prison. By April 7, he was aboard a deportation flight to Mexico.

The country sending him away was his own.

Morales García was born in Denver, according to a copy of his birth certificate reviewed by USA TODAY.

He is part of a long, largely uncounted history of U.S. citizens swallowed by the nation's immigration system. The federal government does not release data on how often its agents detain or deport U.S. citizens, but investigations by journalists, researchers and oversight agencies have documented thousands of citizens detained, deported or otherwise targeted by immigration authorities across decades. One study estimated that U.S. citizens account for as many as 1.5% of all deportees.

A Government Accountability Office report from 2021 offers one glimpse of how often Americans may become entangled in immigration enforcement. Between fiscal year 2015 and the first two quarters of fiscal year 2020, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested 674 potential U.S. citizens, detained 121 and deported 70, according to the report. The majority of those deportations — 66 people — occurred during President Donald Trump's first term.

Yet, even those numbers do not tell the full story. The watchdog agency found that ICE did not consistently track cases involving potential U.S. citizens, making it impossible to know how many people were actually swept into the system.

The problem has persisted through successive Republican and Democratic administrations. Now, experts fear a persistent failure is colliding with a rapid expansion of immigration enforcement — one pushed to deliver record numbers of arrests, increasingly aided by state and local police and operating with fewer internal checks. The result, they warn, is that more citizens could be swept into the dragnet and have fewer places to turn once they are.

"This is a system that is advancing with less accountability now than before," said Jacqueline Stevens, a political science professor at Northwestern University and founder of the school's Deportation Research Clinic. "And less oversight because they're not producing the records that they should be producing on these cases."

Citizens represent a sliver of those targeted by immigration authorities. But for those who are wrongfully detained or deported, the experience can leave lasting trauma, mounting legal costs and consequences that take years to resolve.

For Morales García, returning home required a federal lawsuit — and nearly five months outside his own country.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to USA TODAY's requests for comment. The Department of Justice declined to comment on Morales García's case, citing pending litigation. In court filings, however, the government said Morales García told federal agents he was born in Mexico and freely chose to return there.

In 2001, Morales García was born in Denver to two young Mexican parents who had come to the United States in search of better opportunities. Later that year, he was baptized at St. Therese Catholic Church in Aurora, Colorado, where a baptismal record lists Denver as his birthplace. Morales García also has a Social Security card, a copy of which USA TODAY reviewed. Like cards issued to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, his bears no restriction requiring DHS authorization to work.

But the family's life in the United States was brief. After Morales García's younger brother was born in 2002, his parents returned to Mexico to raise their sons close to family, said his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. Morales García would spend most of the next two decades there, growing up speaking Spanish and eventually getting married.

As he prepared to become a father, Morales García returned to the United States to find work and support his growing family in Mexico, including his wife who was pregnant with their first daughter. He drove north from Aguascalientes — a sunbaked city in Mexico's central highlands — in January 2025. At the port of entry, Morales García showed a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer his Colorado birth certificate, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. The officer let him through.

He settled in Austin, moving through a series of construction jobs before landing one installing air-conditioning units.

On April 3, he was riding to one of those jobs when Texas Department of Public Safety troopers stopped his employer's pickup near Fredericksburg for an alleged window tint violation, according to the federal lawsuit his attorneys later filed. No one in the truck received a citation as a result of the stop, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Morales García repeatedly told the state troopers — and, later, the Gillespie County sheriff's deputies who were called in to translate — that he is American. He explained in Spanish that he had been born in Denver and asked for an opportunity to retrieve his documents, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

The officers, however, contacted ICE. The agency instructed them to hold Morales García and another passenger, according to the lawsuit, and Morales García was booked into the Gillespie County Jail. Both Texas DPS and the Gillespie County Sheriff's Office have formal partnerships with ICE, part of a growing network of state and local agencies enlisted to help enforce federal immigration law.

"There's no law in this country that says that U.S. citizens have to have ID on them when they're going out or riding as passengers in a car," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. "What's happening in the streets is that DPS, ICE and all the sheriffs are just stopping people with brown skin and asking them what their status is, and if they don't have an answer that they like, they're taking them. And it's quiet and it's silent what they're doing, but it's a slippery slope."

Morales García was ultimately transferred into CBP custody. There, Lincoln-Goldfinch said, agents ridiculed his repeated claims that he was American and warned that, if he continued making them, he could face as many as five years in prison.

"At that point, he'd been abused for four days straight, and he believed that he was going to either sign the paperwork they told him to sign or go to jail for years," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. "So he signed these documents... under duress."

With his signature, Morales García had agreed to be deported to Mexico.

Morales García's ordeal fits a pattern Stevens, the political scientist, has spent decades tracing. Some people discover only after they are detained that they have a claim to U.S. citizenship. Others, like Morales García, know they are American from the beginning, yet watch as officers dismiss their claims and the deportation process moves forward anyway.

Stevens calls these cases "the 900-pound gorilla in the coal mine."

"I study U.S. citizens not because I care more about U.S. citizens being wrongfully deported than anybody else," she said. "But if even U.S. citizens can't survive the lawlessness of the deportation process, that tells us a lot about what's happening to everybody else."

Claims of citizenship are supposed to interrupt the machinery of deportation. Federal regulations require unresolved claims to be referred to immigration court. ICE policy also requires officers to consult supervisors and attorneys to put their findings in writing. If the evidence suggests the person might be American — even inconclusively — they should be released while the government decides.

Whether those safeguards were followed in Morales García's case remains unclear.

Still, the 2021 GAO investigation found that the protections were unevenly understood and applied. Some ICE officers had not been trained to follow the agency's own guidance, and neither ICE nor CBP reliably tracked every citizen that's been detained or removed, the report found. Agents are also not required to correct their databases if someone they investigated turned out to be a citizen.

On paper, it's the government's job to prove that someone is not a citizen. In reality, Stevens said, the burden often flips — a result, in part, of Supreme Court rulings that have given immigration authorities broad power and few judicial checks, she said.

Yet, what feels different now, Stevens said, is DHS's growing willingness to double down even after evidence of citizenship emerges.

"Information that's consistent with deportation is treated as accurate," she said. "And information that's inconsistent with deportation is treated as inaccurate and fraudulent."

Last year, 22-year-old Dulce Consuelo Diaz Morales spent 25 days in ICE custody while DHS challenged her Maryland birth certificate. Months later, she received a U.S. passport, and the government dropped its effort to deport her, the Baltimore Banner reported. In Florida, Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez, 20, remained jailed even after a judge verified that he was American, while DHS maintained that he had told officers he was undocumented, according to the Oklahoma Voice.

From Mexico, Morales García could do little more than wait while his attorneys tried to reconstruct the paper trail of his life. In May, they filed a federal lawsuit accusing federal, state and local officials of violating his constitutional rights and asking a judge to order the government to bring him home.

Three weeks after Morales García's attorneys sued, the government told a different story.

In a May 21 court filing, Justice Department attorneys said Morales García initially claimed citizenship and told a Border Patrol agent that he had entered the country with a birth certificate. But after the agent warned him that lying could bring criminal charges, they wrote, Morales García stated that he had been born in Zacatecas.

The DOJ denied that he was threatened or coerced, stating in court documents that he freely signed documents requesting a voluntary return to Mexico. It also pointed to Mexican records bearing another birth date, the spelling "Bryan" and an identity code associated with Zacatecas, Mexico.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Morales García's mother registered his birth in Mexico in 2004. The registrar, according to the family, entered a different date and changed "Brian" to "Bryan," a spelling more commonly used there. Having records in two countries — and discrepancies between them — is common among dual citizens, both Lincoln-Goldfinch and Stevens said.

After nearly five months — and a growing file of evidence — the Justice Department agreed to let Morales García return to the United States, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

On Aug. 30, after a bus ride north from Aguascalientes, Morales García found himself at the border once more. In his hands was the Colorado birth certificate his lawyers had spent months trying to make the government believe. This time, it was enough.

On the other side, his attorneys took him to Starbucks for coffee.

But coming back did not erase what had happened, Morales García said, alleging officers had judged him by how he looked and by the English he could not speak. He worried another traffic stop could end the same way.

"That fear will always be with me," he said in Spanish during a news conference. "It happened once and it can happen a second time."

His return did not end the lawsuit. Richard "Dicky" Grigg, one of his attorneys, said they plan to seek damages to keep other citizens from going through the same ordeal.

"They sent this man, a U.S. citizen, to Mexico, took four months of his life and then let him back in the United States when they realized they'd made a mistake," Grigg said. "To prevent this from happening in the future, we're going to do what we can to make sure government officials, state and federal, are held accountable and responsible."

Morales García's own plans are simpler. He wants to return to work and do what he came to the United States to do in the first place.

"Echarle ganas," he said — to keep going, keep working and keep giving it his all.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Born here but deported. A Texas man's harrowing ordeal.

title: Students divided over University of Michigan hiding first-semester grades for 2027 freshmen
description: University of Michigan students clash over a pass/fail policy hiding first-semester freshman grades, debating mental health relief versus study habits.
fullText:
ANN ARBOR, Mich. — University of Michigan students are split over a new administrative policy that will hide first-semester letter grades for incoming freshmen.

Some welcome the relief from academic pressure while others warn it could coddle students and fail to prepare them for the real world.

Starting in fall 2027, incoming first-year students enrolled in the university's College of Literature, Science, and the Arts (LSA) will have their first-semester transcript grades designated strictly as pass (P) or no credit (NC).

College Students Express Strong Trust In School Leaders Despite Broader Public Cynicism: Gallup

School officials say the pilot program aims to combat a growing "mental health crisis" on college campuses and ease the transition from high school to college.

"Our goal is to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys — core elements of a liberal arts and sciences education," the university stated in its announcement.

While students will still receive traditional letter grades and feedback directly from professors throughout the term, final marks will not appear on official external transcripts or factor into overall GPAs. The university will retain internal letter grade records for advising, financial aid eligibility, academic awards and scholarships and other administrative purposes.

Several students told Fox News Digital that easing into college expectations could be a net positive.

"If there are measures to ease the way for high school students coming to [college], I think that's a good thing," said Alexander, an exchange grad student from Austria.

Ella Langlois, an LSA student, said it does not hurt to give the policy a test run.

"I do think mental health is always super important," she said.

William Bushey, a civil engineering major, called the decision a "good call."

"I'm an engineer, so I go through all the weeder classes all the time," Bushey said. "There's a lot of successful people who struggle in their first-year classes but will just pass and then wind up being super successful later on."

Chloe Song, an economics freshman, agreed that the initial transition can be daunting.

"I think that's a good call because it's really stressful," Song said.

The LSA is the largest of the university's 19 schools and colleges, serving approximately 19,700 undergraduate students. University leaders hope the grade-covering policy gives students the freedom to explore challenging electives without fear of damaging their long-term GPAs.

Similar pass/fail or hidden-grade policies for first-year students have existed for decades at institutions such as Mit, Caltech, Wellesley and Swarthmore.

However, not all Michigan students are on board. Some argue that shielding grading consequences promotes poor study habits and ignores the root causes of student anxiety.

"I think it's kind of silly," said Talan, a freshman neuroscience major. "I know they say it's to curb mental health and stop people from having mental health crises, but I feel like that is our generation having access to media across the world. That's why their mental health is a little worse, not because they're worried about grades.

"We're at the University of Michigan. People tried pretty hard to get here," Talan added. "I feel like grades are taken pretty seriously. And if you're going to try, working as hard as someone who gets a C and passes with the same grade as you is kind of demeaning in a way."

Simran, a sophomore business major, suggested that hiding grades avoids teaching resilience.

"I think having more supportive resources is a better solution than hiding grades," Simran said. "I think there's a lot of challenges that you face in college, and challenging coursework is one of them. It's something you just learn to move through. I've definitely done poorly in classes before, but it's an upward battle at times. … It's a very important skill to have."

Others expressed concern the policy will merely delay academic stress until the second semester.

Andrew Spencer, a biology, health and society major, said that while he might have personally benefited from the break, he believes the policy will ultimately backfire.

"Overall, it's just going to hurt more," Spencer said. "People are just going to slack off and not care about their grades in the first semester and then not have the skills themselves for the second semester to come in and have a great work ethic."

Monica Diaz, a junior studying psychology and economics, offered a middle ground, noting that while she understands critics' concerns, the single-semester policy isn't permanent coddling.

"I don't entirely agree with that because I think it's just slowly transitioning them into what it's like to be at a school like the University of Michigan," Diaz said.

"Obviously, after the first semester, they're not going to be coddled anymore, so I don't really think that's entirely true. But I can definitely see the argument."

title: Texas Republican: ‘I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy’
description: Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense’s argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally r...
fullText:
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense's argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"I don't have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy," Gill said Friday on Fox News's "The Will Cain Show."

"I have an enormous amount of sympathy for the three little innocent kids who were slaughtered," he said earlier.

Gill went on to push back against the central argument of Clancy's defense: that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — at the family's Massachusetts home in 2023.

"You don't get licensed to murder your children or anybody else just because you have mental health problems," Gill said. "We've gotten in a habit of medicalizing evil."

Trial Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when jurors remained deadlocked for seven days without being able to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.

A last-minute attempt was made by Clancy's attorneys to remove the lone holdout juror, whom they accused of refusing to properly apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to remove the juror.

The legal battle has dominated national headlines, with even President Trump weighing in to respond to news of the mistrial.

"It's a shame. It's a horrible tragedy," Trump said when asked about the case during an executive order signing ceremony in the Oval Office. "She did a horrible, horrible thing."

"I guess they're going to go through another trial. It's too bad," he concluded.

title: Like Jamie Dimon, AT&T CEO says if you attend a meeting, you need to show up prepared—he ‘craves’ people who don’t just sit back and observe
description: AT&T’s John Stankey and JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon agree: Meetings should be worth everyone’s time—and attendees shouldn’t be afraid to disagree.
fullText:
Surrounding yourself with a bunch of yes-men is not a recipe for success—at least according to AT&T CEO John Stankey. Instead, he wants employees to come to meetings prepared to share their ideas and perspectives—not simply sit back and listen.

"I love discourse," Stankey said in a recent joint interview with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon hosted by LinkedIn. The telecommunications executive added that one of the principles in his company's cultural documents is to not show up to meetings without having done your homework.

How are AI tools changing meeting preparation?

How do company performances compare under these approaches?

What meeting culture principles do these CEOs follow?

What leadership styles do Stankey and Dimon advocate?

"Don't walk in there and just be an observer," Stankey said. "When you have a point of view, it shouldn't just be some uninformed opinion. It should be a point of view that's built on facts, information, and data. I crave that."

If employees aren't willing to speak up—or don't have a constructive point to make—Stankey suggested there may not be the right people in the room.

Dimon has similarly emphasized the importance of making sure meetings are both necessary and productive. Leaders should create an environment where employees aren't afraid to disagree or raise uncomfortable issues in meetings—even if that means putting the proverbial "dead cat on the table," he said.

"I am never upset when someone says I'm wrong about something," Dimon added. "I just want to do the best I can for our clients, our country, our company."

That leadership strategy has had varying results for the two companies. JPMorgan's stock is up more than 17% over the past year, while AT&T's has fallen about 12%.

The two Fortune 500 CEOs also discussed how they're preparing for meetings in the age of AI. Both have long highlighted the importance of pre-reading materials, but Stankey and Dimon suggested that approach may be changing.

"I'm starting to wonder if reading is the best way to go," Stankey said. "As I've gotten more into the dialog dynamic with AI, I can consume, I think, faster now in a directed conversation."

"I do that same thing," Dimon added. "I use Gemini or Google, and deep dive to get information very quickly. I try to do all my previews before I go to meetings."

Still, the underlying principle hasn't changed: Dimon has long argued that showing up prepared is essential.

"When I go to a meeting, I've done the pre-reads, and you get 100% of my attention," he said at Fortune's Most Powerful Women conference last year. Otherwise, Dimon believes in eliminating meetings altogether when they aren't a productive use of employees' time.

title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
description: Planning, organising and remembering household tasks falls disproportionately to mothers - here are some tips to help.
fullText:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

In a survey looking into the mental load that involved 3,000 US parents, academics at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne found that mothers handled 71% of household tasks that required mental effort, such as keeping track of when sheets and towels needed to be washed and remembering by when food in the fridge needed to be eaten.

The study found that fathers handled many of the tasks researchers described as "episodic" - things that happen less often, such as remembering when to get the car serviced.

University of Melbourne Prof Leah Ruppaner describes the mental load as being invisible, enduring and without boundaries. "You don't bring your dishes to work, but you bring the mental load everywhere," she says.

The mental load is a popular topic on forums like Reddit and Mumsnet, where women seek advice about how to talk to their partners about the exhaustion of trying to juggle so many different responsibilities.

Mums told BBC News they were often added to school WhatsApp groups - where parents discuss things like non-uniform days, school trips, birthdays and lost property - as the "default parent", while their partners never joined.

Sophia, a 35-year-old mum of three in Portsmouth, pays for school trips and makes lunch orders on her children's school's app on her phone, but says her husband has never downloaded it.

Sophia says she tried multiple times to explain the concept of the mental load to her husband - but feels he didn't understand and dismissed her concerns as "quick tasks".

"They are quick tasks if you could just do the task," Sophia says, "but I have to plan for the task, I have to anticipate the task, I have to be 10 steps ahead all the time."

Sam Berry, a deputy headteacher, content creator and married dad of two in London, says when his wife first raised the idea of mental load after his eldest was born, he "didn't really get it" and was "a bit defensive" because he thought he was doing a lot - changing nappies, feeding the baby and more.

He would ask what he could do to help, but he says that still puts the burden on the other person to do the thinking.

As Stacie explains: "I always say to my partner: 'If I have to ask you to do something, that's just adding to my mental load'."

It took a few months of talking and listening for Sam to understand that it was not only about completing the task, but the thinking around it - not just cooking dinner, but what food was in the house, planning the meal, and doing the shopping.

Clinical psychologist Natasha Wallace says some women come to her feeling stressed by the pressure they feel to organise their households.

"It's often, for them, not one enormous stressor," she says. "It's when they realise that they have hundreds of tiny demands on them and their brains and bodies just can't switch off."

Many women are running on autopilot, she adds, so they often don't realise the extent of the cognitive load they're carrying, and this constant low-level stress can have an effect on the nervous system. In turn, this can cause poor sleep, irritability and decision fatigue, she says.

Anita Cleare, parenting expert and author of The Work/Parent Switch, said the overall cognitive drain spills over into our work lives and leads to unsustainable burnout.

One piece of research found that men who earned more did less physical and cognitive labour related to the household, but that when women's earnings increase, they do less physical housework but still the same amount of cognitive labour.

Women very seldomly feel it is a choice to opt out of family life, so the choice then becomes whether to decelerate their career, go part-time, or stop and stay home - with more and more women making that decision, Cleare says.

"If you lower the domestic load, if you lower the mental load, you will create energy, capacity, interest in being able to perform more and better at work."

Many of the women the BBC interviewed said they believed the disparity began with maternity leave.

Wallace says that because women typically take much longer for maternity leave than dads do for paternity leave, they become the "default parent" very early on.

"If you become the person who knows everything, knows where everything is and has in the past done everything, everybody starts coming to you for everything," she says, "so you remain that central person even if you return to work."

In the UK, mothers can take up to 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave, 39 of which can be paid, while fathers can take up to two weeks of leave with statutory paternity pay. Parents can also take shared parental leave.

Some employers offer extra parental leave to their workers, but most people earn less when on maternity or paternity leave, which affects how much leave many fathers take.

Cleare says workplaces can help by making examples of fathers taking paternity leave, not just offering it, and by setting expectations around when employees are contactable, and supporting career conversations for women.

It can also come down to what are seen as traditional roles.

Zach Watson, a married father of three and coach in the US on sharing the mental load, says his grandfather might never have cooked a meal in his married life, while his father did only a little.

In the first five years of his marriage, his wife cooked most of the time. If he offered to cook, he would ask her what she wanted - a question that could actually add to her mental load.

He learned he could come to her with options for dinner, having already looked in the fridge, and give her a default if she wanted to opt entirely out of decision-making. And if he needed help, instead of just asking "Where's the ketchup?", he could explain where he had already looked.

Sam Berry says while some men do not care, a big group - his audience online - "actually are really good husbands, are really good dads, they are trying their best and want to do the best they can, but almost haven't seen it or don't have the language".

Many women the BBC spoke to were keen for their partners to take ownership of certain tasks.

Sam calls this taking on "a category of tasks" - so dad might handle all the school admin, while mum manages the food.

However, he says equality is not necessarily about splitting everything 50/50 - because one partner might work more and another might like cooking - but about finding what works best for both partners.

And if you traditionally hold more of the mental load, you might need to accept that your partner may do things very differently, and it might not always go smoothly, says Afua Williams, 40, a mother of two in London.

Those who spoke to BBC News shared their own tips about how to manage the mental load equally:

Communicate clearly with your partner about how you're feeling and the impact of your mental load. Zach calls it "labelling" - making the invisible cognitive and emotional labour visible. Don't have these conversations when you're feeling angry or overwhelmed, says Wallace, or it can feel like the other person is being "blamed or criticised"

"See what you can offload", says Ana Catalano Weeks, co-author of a study on how mental load impacts work. Do you really need to organise physical birthday cards for your children's friends? Can you mute parents' WhatsApp groups and just focus on official school emails?

Have regular check-ins with your partner - it could be daily, weekly, or seasonally

Create a shared calendar so that everyone is aware of birthdays, school meetings and more

Take ownership of tasks from start to finish without the need to be reminded, Wallace says

Don't fall into the "efficiency trap" that the solution is just to be more organised, Cleare says. Remember that what matters most as a parent are moments of connection with your child - not eating certain vegetables - and that will help redefine expectations

title: Casey beaten on fourth play-off hole in Switzerland
description: England's Paul Casey is beaten by South Africa's defending champion Thriston Lawrence on the fourth play-off hole at the European Masters in Switzerland.
fullText:
European Masters, final leaderboard

-18 P Casey (Eng), T Lawrence*; -17 H Hall; -16 F Laporta (Ita), A Ayora (Spa), A Hidalgo (Spa), B Wiesberger (Aut), E Lopez-Chacarra (Spa)

Selected others: -15 M Wallace (Eng); -14 R Hoejgaard (Den), P Reed (US); -13 T Clements (Eng); -11 M Penge (Eng); -9 C Hill (Sco), S Garcia (Spa)

Paul Casey was beaten by South Africa's defending champion Thriston Lawrence on the fourth play-off hole at the European Masters in Switzerland.

The tournament was played at the Crans-sur-Sierre Golf Club in Crans-Montana, and Casey had pledged to donate his entire winnings to the victims of the New Year's Eve fire that killed 40 people in the Swiss mountain resort.

The 49-year-old Englishman missed four putts for the first prize of $637,500 (£469,112) - the first on his final hole in regulation and the next three on the first three play-off holes.

But after firing his approach to the back edge of the green at the fourth play-off hole, the former Ryder Cup player missed a chip and Lawrence sank his birdie putt to win the tournament for the third time - equalling the record of Seve Ballesteros.

Casey fired a two-under-par 68 in his final round to finish level on 18 under, with Lawrence forcing a play-off thanks to a stunning 62.

The LIV player was aiming for his 16th win on the DP World Tour and first since he claimed the Dubai Desert Classic in January 2021, but after finishing just short will now donate the runners-up prize of $412,500 (£303,543) to the Fondation Beloved, external.

England's Harry Hall finished third on 17 under after his closing 63.

Swiss regions ban pyrotechnics after ski bar fire

Casey secures Dubai Desert Classic title

"It's probably the most emotion I have ever shown in a happy way," said Lawrence, who hit eight birdies in a bogey-free round to set the clubhouse lead on 18 under.

"I fought so hard and just gave it my everything. I feel for Paul, he played great golf and it looked like it was his all day, even in the play-off. He missed a couple of short ones, but it's just the best feeling in the world."

Casey started the day six shots ahead of Lawrence, but struggled to rekindle the form that saw him hit 64 and 63 in his second and third rounds.

The LIV golfer dropped shots on three of his opening eight holes, including a double bogey six on the sixth.

Casey was two over for the day after a bogey on the eighth, but then picked up five birdies in the next seven holes to reclaim the lead.

The world number 707 made it up and down from a greenside bunker to save par on the 16th, then narrowly missed another birdie putt on the 17th to leave himself needing a par on the last for victory.

But he was unable to navigate the par four 18th safely after finding thick rough from the tee. Casey bounced his approach off a rock and over a stream into the rough guarding the green and after a poor chip shot missed a 20-foot putt for victory.

The difficult 18th hole was chosen for the play-off.

Both golfers made pars in their first two attempts, with Casey missing a 10-foot birdie putt to win on the second play-off hole.

Tournament organisers changed the pin position for the third play-off hole in an attempt to separate the two, but again they both made pars, with Casey seeing his eight-foot putt for the championship hit the cup and roll out.

And Lawrence finally punished his opponent on the fourth play-off hole.

title: Wellens wins Tour of Britain as GB's Askey finishes second
description: Belgium's Tim Wellens wins the 2026 Tour of Britain as Nils Politt claims victory on stage five.
fullText:
Belgium's Tim Wellens won the 2026 Tour of Britain as Nils Politt claimed victory on stage five.

Wellens began the day with a 21 second lead over Great Britain's Lewis Askey and extended that to 42 seconds as he finished eighth, 21 seconds behind German Politt, on the final stage.

Askey finished 40 seconds adrift of Wellens on the 156.1km run through Earlston but managed to hold on to second place, with Belgium's Jasper Stuyven 21 seconds behind him in third place.

Great Britain's Elliot Rowe ended the event in sixth place, with compatriots Mark Donovan in ninth and Ben Wiggins in 10th.

Prior to the start of the stage, the riders gave Briton Ben Swift a guard of honour as the 38-year-old recently announced he will retire at the end of the 2026 season.

Politt launched an attack with just under nine kilometres to go and saw off Wiggins before going on to win his first stage since 2022.

Meanwhile, on the shortened stage 15 of the Vuelta a Espana, Wout van Aert claimed an impressive victory.

During the tactical latter stages, Van Aert - who won stage 13 - covered any attacks from his rivals in a five-rider breakaway before he proved strongest in a sprint for the line in Cordoba.

The stage had been shortened from 189.7km to 110.2km as race organisers had activated the extreme weather protocol because of the heat and temperatures reached 40C.

Enric Mas retained the overall leader's red jersey as second-placed Felix Gall stays two minutes and six seconds adrift, while Primoz Roglic is 2:10 behind the leader going into Monday's rest day.

title: New contenders emerge on WSL return - but Man City start strong
description: The Women’s Super League returned this weekend and with it a host of new signings, improved squads and unexpected results.
fullText:
The Women’s Super League returned this weekend and with it a host of new signings, improved squads and unexpected results.

Manchester City began the defence of their title with victory at home to newly-promoted Birmingham City, while underdogs Crystal Palace upset Everton.

But which clubs made a statement and do Manchester City look like title favourites again?

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

As is the case with any new season, an early look at title challengers does not give the whole story but can be a good marker of who has the right credentials.

There were debuts for big-name signings Ona Batlle and Georgia Stanway at Arsenal, while Katie McCabe swapped red for blue when she started for Chelsea.

Manchester City also had new faces off the bench as they navigated an injury-hit squad on opening weekend.

But the reigning champions could not have hoped for a better start as they hosted WSL 2 winners Birmingham at the Joie Stadium and cruised to a 3-1 victory.

It was an assured display, full of the attacking flair and threat they unleashed last season with the only criticism that they should have scored more.

Birmingham City were no pushovers and performed well on their return to the top flight, but Andree Jeglertz’s side still imposed their superiority.

The Swedish boss was delighted with victory, though the perfectionist in him wanted more after a "hesitant" first half.

"In the first half, it was almost [like we were] getting into it again. We turned it around and the second half was much smoother," said Jeglertz.

"It's about driving the game and we did that. Even though we scored goals, we wanted more."

New season, same flaw - Chelsea title hopes already under scrutiny

Manchester City did what Chelsea could not as Sonia Bompastor's side were held to a frustrating 1-1 draw by Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge.

Despite 57 touches in the opposition box, 23 shots inside the area, an effort that hit the crossbar and a disallowed goal for offside, Chelsea could not break Villa down.

Their lack of ruthlessness was a consistent characteristic last season as Chelsea, who had won the previous six WSL titles, fell to third in the table.

Their opening display did little to ease concerns it would be a similar story this season, while City showed they remain a serious force to overcome.

Elsewhere, the bookies' favourites to win the league, Arsenal, did not find life easy at Brighton for their opening game.

Arturo Ruiz, 29, took charge of his first match for Albion - a side many think can challenge the WSL's giants - and they made life tough for the Gunners.

A moment of quality from 19-year-old Lisa Baum on her Arsenal debut won the points in a 1-0 victory and, while unconvincing, it remains early days.

Last season's Champions League quarter-finalists Manchester United did not get off to a good start under manager Eva Olid as they were beaten by a surprisingly fluid display from opponents London City Lionesses on Friday.

The team of superstars, boosted by new signings such as two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and Spain defender Mapi Leon, lived up to the hype on the opening night to pick up a well-earned 2-1 win.

They had 60% possession and 11 shots - not bad for a team who have barely got to know each other during a high-turnover summer.

While they clearly have bags of talent, there was scepticism at how quickly London City would gel, but on Friday night's showing they could be one of this season's challengers for a Women's Champions League qualification spot.

Superstar-led London City live up to hype as Man Utd suffer

Another contender will be Tottenham.

Martin Ho's side laid strong foundations last season in finishing fifth and they have started this campaign strongly with a 3-1 win over West Ham.

Debutant Kirsty Hanson, who they snatched from Aston Villa after she finished as their top-scorer in 2025-26, hit the ground running with two goals in London.

Perhaps the surprise package of the weekend was Liverpool, who have been busy in the transfer window and looked very strong against newly-promoted Charlton.

Tougher challenges will come their way but Gareth Taylor's side oozed confidence and new signing Vivien Endemann was a standout performer in a 4-0 drubbing.

It took them until January last season to pick up a victory as they battled at the bottom of the table - so they have already laid a marker.

"It feels very, very good. We had a clean sheet, scored four goals and won the first match," goalscorer Endemann told Sky Sports.

"Last season, it was really tough, so now to start with a win is very important for us. We want to keep going."

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace's 1-0 victory over Everton proved there is hope for the promoted sides in the expanded 14-team league, despite those losses for Birmingham and Charlton.

Jo Potter's Palace edged in front in the first half thanks to Lexi Lloyd-Smith's finish and held off Everton, whose only shot on target came in stoppage time.

"No words can explain. I'm buzzing. To get to do this in front of my friends and family, it was an unbelievable feeling," said Lloyd-Smith.

"We knew it was going to be hard, we knew we were going into these games as underdogs. It's so good that in the first game we show we're here to put out a statement.

"I feel like we've got a lot to give."
