title: McColgan wins London Big Half after five months out
description: Britain's Eilish McColgan returns to competitive action after five months out with a broken toe to win the London Big Half for a fourth time.
fullText:
Eilish McColgan claimed her fourth victory at the Big Half in London on Sunday after returning to action following five months out with a fractured foot.

The 35-year-old Scot suffered the injury during the London Marathon in April, crossing the line in seventh place with blood seeping through her shoe, and was forced to pull out of July's Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

But McColgan showed the benefit of months of warm weather training, completing a comfortable victory over the 13.1-mile course back in the English capital.

The British women's half-marathon record holder beat last year's winner Jessica Warner-Judd by one minute 19 seconds, finishing in a time of 1hr 10mins 54secs.

McColgan might have 'one more' Games in her

McColgan to miss Glasgow Games defence after foot fracture

It was more than three minutes outside her best time for the course and well outside her British record for the distance of 1:05:43.

Britain's Jack Rowe missed out on a record fourth consecutive victory in the men's race, finishing in second place, 14 seconds behind Birchfield Harriers' Kadar Omar Abdullahi, who won in a time of 1:01:51.

Britain's David Weir defended his title in the men's wheelchair event, winning the race for the fifth time in its nine-year history in a new record time.

The 47-year-old, who retired from Paralympic competition in 2024, knocked 45 seconds off his own record for the course, which he set last year, winning in 46:13.

Eden Rainbow Cooper won the women's event in 52:47 to defend her title.

title: Police investigate Bielik fan clash at Portsmouth
description: Police are investigating an incident between Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik and a Portsmouth supporter during Pompey's 2-0 home win on Saturday.
fullText:
Police are investigating an incident between Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik and home supporters during Portsmouth's 2-0 Championship win on Saturday.

Bielik was involved in a physical altercation with a fan as he went to retrieve a ball from the crowd late in the second half.

Hampshire Police were notified of the incident during the match and launched an investigation immediately afterwards.

"We can confirm that we are investigating an incident in which a teenage boy was reportedly the victim of a common assault during the football match at Fratton Park. Our enquiries are ongoing," the police said.

Several Portsmouth supporters made gestures that indicated they believed the fan had been grabbed by the throat.

Cardiff head coach Brian Barry-Murphy claimed afterwards that Bielik "got slapped in the face", while clips circulating on social media appeared to show the Poland international grabbing a young fan around his upper body.

In the aftermath, another fan threw a ball at the head of Cardiff defender Perry Ng. Both supporters were ejected from the stadium.

After the game Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho apologised to Cardiff City's players.

Pompey added in a statement:, external "Portsmouth Football Club are aware of supporter concerns regarding the incident involving a young fan and an opposition player at yesterday's match at Fratton Park.

"As this remains a safeguarding matter and is currently under investigation by both the club and the police, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further on the circumstances at this time.

"However, we are aware that a number of claims and assertions are circulating on social media. We would urge caution against speculation while enquiries are ongoing.

"The welfare and safeguarding of young people are of paramount importance to Portsmouth Football Club. We will continue to liaise with the relevant parties as enquiries progress.

"No further comment will be made at this stage while investigations remain ongoing."

The Football Association is aware of the matter and will review the details in the referee's match report before deciding whether any action should be taken.

Cardiff City said: "We are satisfied with the way that match officials dealt with the situation during the game, having been in full view of it. Player protection will always be of paramount importance to us."

title: Fifa president Infantino will stand for re-election
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election in March, the world governing body has confirmed.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election in March, says football's world governing body.

Infantino, who has filled the role since 2016, has been under pressure following his scrapped plan to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment firms.

Infantino's lucrative plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

"The Fifa president announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027," read a Fifa statement.

"Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election."

Infantino refused to answer questions about his future when asked by reporters at the Women's Under-20 World Cup in Poland on Saturday.

It is the first time Fifa has said he will run for a new term since the plan was announced following the summer's World Cup.

Should the 56-year-old Swiss be re-elected, he will serve until 2031.

Fifa this week accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership", in a challenge to litigation over Infantino's plan.

Last week Uefa filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

Division, drama and power - what next for Infantino and Uefa?

As recently as mid-July Infantino was considered a certainty to be re-elected.

All but a handful of Fifa members had endorsed him, and he faced no meaningful challenge.

However, the Football Associations of England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are among those to have publicly withdrawn support since Infantino's plan was announced.

BBC Sport understands Uefa is confident that a candidate can be found to stand against Infantino.

A candidate must receive the backing of at least 106 of the 211 Fifa member associations.

Uefa has abandoned the idea of trying to force a vote of no confidence.

It would require three-quarters of the members - 159 votes - to pass the motion through a change of Fifa statutes, which is considered unrealistic.

No candidates to challenge Infantino have been named, although Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is considered a serious option.

Nominations must be submitted by 18 November.

title: Argentina ratchets up Falklands tensions after Trump casts doubt on support for Britain
description: Argentine President Javier Milei has announced plans to sanction oil companies working near the Falkland Islands, escalating a long-running dispute with Britain days after President Donald Trump said ...
fullText:
Argentine President Javier Milei has announced plans to sanction oil companies working near the Falkland Islands, escalating a long-running dispute with Britain days after President Donald Trump said the US position on the archipelago was "under review."

In an address late Thursday, Milei reasserted Argentina's claim to the islands in the South Atlantic Ocean, which the United Kingdom has controlled since 1833 and over which the two countries fought a war in the early 1980s.

"The Falkland Islands are Argentinian, historically and legally. There is no debate," Milei said, adding that "winds of change" had become more favorable to Argentina's claim.

The right-wing libertarian leader's comments came after Trump suggested earlier this week that Washington could review its long-held position of maintaining strategic ambiguity on the question of the territory's sovereignty, while accepting de facto British rule.

Milei described an oilfield project off the coast of the Falklands, involving Israeli and British firms, as a "concrete and urgent danger" that is advancing toward oil extraction without Argentina's permission.

"If we fail to act, within a few months, they will possess the physical capacity to take the oil reserves that lie beneath our waters."

Milei warned that the oilfield project could "create an incentive for the UK to deepen its occupation" and "continue exploiting our resources."

Britain's foreign minister hit back on Friday, saying the UK's commitment to the Falkland islands was "unwavering" and the right to self-determination was grounded in international law.

"The Islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders," Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on X.

In an interview with The Economist published that same day, Milei expressed his desire for a "consensus solution" with Britain on the islands' future, and referenced the agreement under which Britain returned its former colony Hong Kong to China in 1997.

"In the long term we can get our islands back. The UK did this with Hong Kong, so why not find the agreement so that sooner or later the islands return to Argentina? They're ours," he told the outlet.

CNN has reached out to the UK Foreign Office for comment.

In his latest plan, announced Thursday, Milei called for a law change to allow tougher sanctions on companies providing services to those involved in hydrocarbon exploitation.

The companies behind the oil project – Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration – said the recent developments are not expected to affect their activities.

In a joint statement, they said they have valid licenses to operate, granted by the islands' government with the "full and ongoing" support of the UK.

Milei also announced more resources for the building of a naval base in Tierra del Fuego, Argentina's southernmost territory, which Milei said would strengthen the country's geopolitical influence and position it as a key logistics hub.

The two countries went to war over the territory, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, in 1982 after the then military government in Argentina landed troops on the islands. The conflict claimed the lives of 645 Argentinians and 255 Britons.

The brief war and status of the islands still rankle many Argentinians, and political leaders there are frequently pressured to take up the cause.

The issue came to the fore in July, when Argentine football players held up a banner reading "the Malvinas are Argentine" after beating England in the football World Cup semi-final.

The US has never backed UK sovereignty claims over the area. When troops from Argentina invaded the Falklands in 1982, Britain fought back on its own and did not see traditional allies like the United States or NATO join the campaign.

In an interview aired on Thursday with British broadcaster GB News, Trump avoided directly answering a question about whether the US would "come to the aid" of Britain in another conflict over the Falklands.

"Well look, I was there when they had the first war. That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away. That's a big trip, it's a long way," he said.

He also repeated past complaints that Britain had not provided sufficient support for the US-led bombing campaign against Iran.

"Your country was not there to help me," Trump said, recalling Britain's former prime minister, Keir Starmer, telling him the country did not have ships to contribute to the campaign. "It was pretty sad, the whole thing."

While Britain did not join the US and Israel's war with Iran, it did allow US planes involved in bombing missions to use UK bases. That decision has proved controversial in Britain where – like in much of Europe - there has been very little public appetite to join another US war in the Middle East.

The Falklands, which raise their own taxes but rely on the UK for defense and foreign policy, are one of 14 British Overseas Territories.

Residents of the islands voted to remain under British rule in a 2013 referendum. More than 99% of voters who cast ballots backed that option.

However, Milei said Friday that the population does "not have a legitimate right to self-determination" and that any argument based on a referendum held there "is invalid."

He also praised Trump for suggesting Washington could reconsider its historically neutral stance on the islands' sovereignty, casting the potential shift as proof that his close relationship with the US president was yielding results.

"The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that in Argentina, it has a reliable partner – one aligned with Western values, in a position of strategic importance that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come," Milei said.

CNN's Federico Jofre contributed to this report.

title: Trump signs order to remove endangered species protection for grey wolves
description: The US president says the move will help ranchers, but conservationists say it could derail efforts to recover populations.
fullText:
Donald Trump has signed an executive order to remove endangered species protection for the grey wolf and a subspecies, the Mexican wolf.

The US president's decision could pave the way for pastoral farmers to kill the canines to protect their livestock. His order said ranchers played a "vital role" in the food supply chain and American cultural heritage.

But conservation groups have criticised the move, saying it could derail long-term efforts to recover the endangered wolf populations.

There were 319 Mexican wolves in the wild in the US in 2025, up from just four when they were reintroduced in 1998, US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) figures show.

Meanwhile, there are roughly 18,000 grey wolves across the US, though they are still considered endangered as most of their habitat has been destroyed by humans.

An attempt to de-list them at a federal level in 2022 became tied up in litigation, and some campaigners have indicated they intend to do the same of the US Department of Interior acts on Trump's order.

The executive order does not give ranchers immediate license to shoot wolves preying on livestock, but instead gives Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to determine whether the grey and Mexican wolf populations had recovered enough to warrant being taken off the endangered species list.

Noting that US livestock herds were at a 75-year low while demand for beef had risen by 10% in the past decade, the order added: "More can and should be done to support this critical industry."

However, environmental groups pointed to studies that suggested wolf attacks on livestock were rare and had little impact on ranchers' income.

"This is a huge distraction to placate a handful of ranchers and make them believe that wolves are a greater threat than President Trump's own policies," said Greta Anderson, deputy director of Western Watersheds Project, which works to conserve wildlife in western US states.

The Wolf Conservation Center noted that ranchers were entitled to up to 100% compensation for any livestock losses caused by wolves under the current system, with individual states providing funding for programmes to deter attacks.

"The Mexican grey wolf is not recovered simply because the population has grown," said Claire Musser, executive director of the Grand Canyon Wolf Recovery Project. "Weakening federal protections now would put decades of recovery work at risk."

The executive order comes as the Trump administration is seeking to lower record-high beef prices for consumers, driven by drought and an outbreak of parasites in US beef stocks.

Ranchers have been frustrated by Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on beef imports to address price rises, putting pressure on their already tight margins.

The US government launched a campaign to systematically exterminate wolves towards the end of the 19th Century. This, along with farmers and landowners trapping and killing wolves, pushed them to the brink of eradication.

Ranchers still view them as a nuisance, which tackling lethally constitutes a federal crime.

title: Green Party deputy leader linked to property lets despite opposition to landlords
description: Mothin Ali, is linked to two rental properties via his company, but does not appear to profit from them.
fullText:
The deputy leader of the Green Party, Mothin Ali, is linked to two buy-to-let properties, despite his party's opposition to private landlords.

Ali is the sole director of a company, which he set up and controls, that owns two rental properties in Leeds, bought in June 2022 and March 2025 - although he does not appear to profit from either of them.

The property purchases happened before the Greens adopted a policy committing to phasing out ownership of rental properties by private landlords in October 2025.

The Green Party told the BBC that, at the time Ali had set up the company, and since, he "has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities".

Ali's connection to the rental properties via real estate company MA Holdings, which purchased them with buy-to-let mortgages, was first reported by the Times newspaper.

Records held by Companies House show that Ali is the sole director of MA Holdings, incorporated in December 2021, and he is listed in the records as the sole person with significant control, owning more than 75% of the shares.

The company's business includes "buying and selling of own real estate", "letting and operating of own or leased real estate" and "management of real estate on a fee or contract basis".

The BBC has spoken to the previous owner and resident of the second property, who confirmed that Ali's company had purchased the property and believed it was bought with the intention to be let out.

Asked why MA Holdings owns the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson said: "We have provided deeply personal information to the BBC in confidence which shows that Councillor Ali has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities.

"At Councillor Ali's request, we are not going to make this information public to protect his family."

The BBC is not publicising the personal information shared with it, at the request of the Greens, as it relates to private family matters.

In October last year, delegates to the Green Party's annual conference, passed a motion titled "Abolish landlords", headed "the private rental sector has failed, it is a vehicle for wealth extraction, funnelling money from renters to the landlord class".

The motion states: "The effective abolition of private landlordism and the private rented sector, coupled with the mass expansion of council housing, is the only way to end the housing crisis."

This is now official policy for the Green Party of England and Wales, with a plan to increase regulation and taxes on private rentals to make it difficult for landlords to make a profit, while boosting housebuilding by councils.

The policy would use existing Green policies such as imposing rent controls, ending buy-to-let mortgages and giving councils the right to buy a rental property when it is sold at a discounted price.

Asked whether Ali had sought to take any steps since the policy had been adopted to change anything with regard to the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson told the BBC he fully supported the policy.

"The policy does not literally seek to abolish landlords, but rather to put in more regulations and taxes on private rentals through measures such as rent controls and expanded social housing," they said. "All of which Mothin Ali supports."

When the policy was introduced, Green Party MP Carla Denyer told the BBC "while the motion to conference had an eye-catching name, it does not actually 'abolish' landlords".

"It does, however, address the housing crisis, empowers tenants and improves their wellbeing," she added.

"It contains a range of policies which, over time, would reduce the proportion of the housing market that is privately rented, and increase the proportion of socially rented homes."

New study links artificial sweetener to heart attack, stroke risk
description: Xylitol is present in some baked goods, nut butters and ice creams.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — A new study by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) has found an association between artificial sweetener xylitol and an increased risk of heart attack and stroke. The findings were presented at the ESC Conference 2026.

Xylitol is a compound commonly used as a sugar substitute, as it has fewer calories and less of an effect on a person's blood sugar. It is in some natural foods, like fruits. Xylitol can also be produced naturally in the body due to glucose metabolism.

According to a release, xylitol is often added in amounts over a thousand times higher than it's found naturally to oral care products and artificially sweetened foods and beverages. Xylitol is also in some baked goods, nut butters and ice creams, sugar-free gum and candy, as well as chewable vitamins and cough syrups, according to Harvard Health Publishing.

The study looked at two cohorts made up of 17,710 people from Canada and Europe. The study observed, in the Canadian cohort, that people with the highest amount of xylitol in their blood were 57% more at risk for heart attacks and strokes. In the European cohort, people who had the highest levels had an 18% greater risk.

These findings stayed the same when cardiovascular risks like age, smoking status, diabetes, sex, lipid levels and hypertension were factored in. The study suggests that the risk is associated with how much xylitol is in the blood.

"Artificial sweeteners are consumed by people who think they are healthier than sugar and they are generally regarded as safe by regulatory agencies," said Dr. Marco Witkowski, who presented the findings. "Our long-term findings in the general population highlight how little we know about the cardiovascular safety of xylitol and indicate that further studies are warranted, especially as the amount of xylitol in products continues to increase."

Researchers say the findings point to a need for further research into the cardiovascular effects of xylitol.

title: At flood-destroyed border, China teams scour ruins of once-busy port
description: Chinese officials said on Sunday that workers had recovered 12 more bodies as the search continued for hundreds still missing after a
fullText:
GYIRONG, China, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Chinese officials said on Sunday that workers had recovered 12 more bodies as the search continued for hundreds still missing after a tsunami-like mudslide destroyed China's main border crossing with Nepal.

Rescue workers in bright ‌orange uniforms used excavators, shovels and ground-penetrating radar to scour the now-buried site of the Gyirong border crossing.

The border crossing became a grisly ‌emblem of the devastation that followed the collapse of a glacier on the Nepal side of the border on August 26 after videos showed a black wave of water, mud and debris ​sweeping over it with little warning.

The mudslide has killed more than 1,300 people on both sides of the border, with more than 5,000 missing.

On the Chinese side, 43 were confirmed dead and 519 remained missing as of Saturday. Among those still unaccounted for were 261 foreigners from 23 countries, officials said.

There was no trace ‌of the five-storey Chinese customs building that had stood ⁠at the border before the disaster. The only structure still visible was part of a nearby water tower installation in a barren grey-black mud field.

Workers had planted a Chinese flag where the nearly 20-metre-tall border gate once stood.

Behind signs warning "Danger Area ⁠Pass Quickly", groups of rescue and recovery workers dug through the debris while red excavators stood nearby.

Officials told visiting reporters that recovery teams were taking fingerprints and recording identifying features such as tattoos as bodies were recovered. They had also collected 993 personal items from the site.

Families and diplomats representing countries with missing nationals have privately ​expressed ​growing frustration over what they describe as limited information-sharing by China.

Beijing has not detailed how ​it plans to proceed with DNA identification of victims as ‌remains are recovered, representatives of four governments told Reuters.

Diplomats also said China had not answered questions about whether video from the border crossing, including facial-recognition footage, could be shared with families or used to help identify the dead.

China's foreign ministry has said its release of information about the floods was "transparent and timely" and that it is ready to work with other countries and agencies.

Once a historic trading hub, Gyirong had become the main crossing for trade and travellers between Nepal and Tibet after a 2015 earthquake damaged an alternative route farther east.

China will consider whether it should be built back differently in the wake of the ‌disaster, officials said.

The crossing was closed between July last year and January after an earlier ​glacial flood. Alongside serving as a gateway for Chinese exports, including electric vehicles, it had ​become a transit point for Hindu pilgrims travelling through Nepal to Mount ​Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for both Hindus and Buddhists. Hindus believe it to be the eternal home of ‌Lord Shiva and his wife Parvati.

Many of the foreign nationals still ​missing in Tibet were pilgrims with extended ​families in India, diplomats in Beijing have said. There are 49 Indian citizens among the missing.

China has pushed back against any suggestion that it could have provided any further early warning data before the glacier collapse in Nepal.

Chinese scientists have found more than 3,000 glacial lakes, of which ​187 are classified as high-risk and are monitored via remote ‌sensors or on the ground, officials told reporters.

"This disaster occurred on the Nepalese side of the border, further international cooperation is required ​to enhance monitoring and early-warning capabilities," Norbu Tsering, deputy head of the emergency rescue headquarters, said.

(Additional reporting by Ella Cao; Writing by ​Mei Mei Chu and Kevin Krolicki; Editing by Saad Sayeed and Ros Russell)

title: Russia's Lavrov calls accusations of Moscow's involvement in Leipzig drone incident 'start of real war', TASS reports
description: MOSCOW, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Sunday that the accusations levelled at Moscow by the West that it was involved in the drone incident at Germany's Leipzig
fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Sunday ‌that the accusations levelled at ‌Moscow by the West that it was involved ​in the drone incident at Germany's Leipzig airport were, "by and large, the start of a real war," state news ‌agency TASS reported.

"All ⁠these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military ⁠power in Europe once again – they are being put into practice. He ​is, in ​effect, declaring war ​on us," Lavrov ‌said, referring to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The German government said on September 1 that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone ‌attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport ​last month and ordered ​a series ​of measures in response, including ‌the closure of a ​consulate and ​a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.

Russia dismissed the German accusations as baseless, ​accusing ‌Berlin of planting evidence to frame ​Russia for the attack.

title: Turning Point is laying the groundwork to shape Republican presidential primary in 2028
description: Alongside the familiar sounds of roosters crowing and thrill seekers screaming on rides at the Iowa State Fair, there was a chorus of boos from Turning Point Action activists who were heckling Democra...
fullText:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Alongside the familiar sounds of roosters crowing and thrill seekers screaming on rides at the Iowa State Fair, there was a chorus of boos from Turning Point Action activists who were heckling Democratic politicians making their way through the crowds.

Videos of the confrontations got hundreds of thousands of views on social media, a burst of attention for a conservative youth organization that is charting its next chapter after last year's assassination of its leader Charlie Kirk. But the true test of Turning Point Action's clout was unfolding inside the exhibition center, where staff members were registering voters, handing out buttons and signing people up for social events.

"Building the foundation for 2028," said one of the flyers.

While Democrats have punted Iowa from the top of its presidential primary calendar, the state's caucuses will still kick off Republicans' next nominating process. Turning Point Action is positioning itself to shape that contest, a reminder that preparations for the next White House campaign are already in motion even though no candidates have announced and the midterm elections aren't over yet.

Turning Point Action wants at least one staffer in each of Iowa's 99 counties to mobilize the conservative grassroots.

"It is important to us to see high voter participation in the caucuses," said Tyler Bowyer, the organization's chief operating officer. "That's your measuring stick."

In addition to Iowa, Turning Point Action grew its footprint in New Hampshire and Nevada for this year's midterms, which could also help in 2028.

The likely beneficiary of this initiative would be Vice President JD Vance, who is widely expected to launch a campaign. Turning Point leaders including Erika Kirk, Charlie's widow, have been clear they're ready to throw their support behind Vance if he jumps in.

More than a dozen Republican officials, activists, lawmakers and strategists in Iowa said Turning Point's imprint in the state was visible but still something of a mystery, and some privately question whether the organization's impact will match the buzz that it generates online.

But others have eagerly welcomed the organization to the state.

"A year ago, Iowa was virgin — no Turning Point. And many of us complained," said Kelley Koch, a former Dallas County Republican chair, to a gathering of MAGA Nation Iowa, the grassroots organization she founded. "Finally, Turning Point Action listened to us."

When asked about his 2028 ambitions, Vance demurs and says he's focused on his current job, but he's expected to be an immediate Republican frontrunner if he decides to seek the presidency. Bowyer said Turning Point Action wants to be supportive without "being pushy."

"We haven't officially endorsed as an organization yet because no one's announced, right? But, you know, depending on who announces and when we endorse — yeah, of course we'll be out campaigning on behalf of who we endorse," he said.

Bowyer said Vance can bridge the gap between the Make America Great Again movement, which Trump launched more than a decade ago, and younger voters who were attracted to Charlie Kirk's brand of conservatism.

Bowyer acknowledged that Turning Point Action's growing infrastructure in early primary states could cause some agitation on the right if it is seen as throwing its weight behind one presidential candidate. But, he said "that's not why we do it," describing the goal as boosting turnout in the Iowa caucuses to send a strong signal heading into the general election.

Other potential candidates include Marco Rubio, Trump's secretary of state. However, Rubio has said he wouldn't run against Vance.

Sen. Ted Cruz has not announced a campaign, but he has already made several visits to Iowa this year and said in a recent podcast hosted by Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick that, "It's no secret that I want to be president."

Although Iowa has shifted rightward over the last decade, it's considered a political battleground in this year's midterm elections because of Trump's sagging approval ratings, declining access to healthcare and tariff-driven turmoil in the agricultural industry.

Sen. Joni Ernst and Gov. Kim Reynolds, both Republicans, are retiring, and there are fiercely contested races to replace them. Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson are seeking the Senate seat, while Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn want to be governor. Two battleground congressional districts will help determine control of the House as well.

The spotlight on Iowa this year is an opportunity for Turning Point Action to demonstrate its clout.

The organization said it hired four staffers on the ground last year. After Lahn's surprise win over Trump-endorsed Rep. Randy Feenstra, Turning Point Action said it would double its manpower in the state before the midterms.

Young activists regularly post on social media from county fairs and Republican committee meetings. They upload selfies on sidewalks or stoops to show days spent knocking on doors.

"We're newer in Iowa," a Des Moines-based senior field staffer, Kylie Kloewer, told a visitor who stopped by Turning Point Action's booth at the state fair.

The booth featured signs emphasizing that there are only two genders and one that said "men can't get pregnant," the kind of confrontational culture war messaging that Charlie Kirk practiced on college campuses. Some people nodded and chuckled, while others raised their eyebrows as they wandered by.

Those who walked up to the table could 

"Any involvement is success," said Kelsey Newberry, who is based in the organization's Phoenix headquarters and was helping at the Iowa State Fair. "You're bringing people together as a community. The more you talk to your neighbors, the better."

"And even if they're not ready to get activated now," Newberry added, "being around like-minded people might encourage them in the future."

Price reported from Washington.

title: Abdul El-Sayed hits back at Israel questions, suggests his name and faith are behind press scrutiny
description: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed suggested reporters press him on the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and faith.
fullText:
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed suggested that reporters press him about the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and his faith.

"You've been asked many times whether you support a two-state solution regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and you generally say you support equal rights to self-determination for Jewish Israelis and Palestinians," Gorchow said. "Can you tell us, what does that mean?"

Michigan Dem Hopeful Abdul El-sayed Jabs Cnn Giving Him 'Non-consensual Colonoscopy' In Recent Interviews

Michigan Senate Candidate Confronted Repeatedly Over Israel's Right To Exist, Defunding The Police

Michigan Senate Hopeful Calls Aipac Donations 'Legalized Bribery,' Remains Silent On Other Donations

El-sayed's Hasan Piker Problem Follows Him To Dem Convention As Jewish Voters Break Ranks

Michigan Democratic Senate Candidate Claims Israel 'Just As Evil' As Hamas

"It's fascinating to me that I'm running to represent 10 million people who live here, and you want to ask about people living somewhere else," El-Sayed continued. "And I just think I want to be talking about [the] people living here."

Jewish Democrats Abandon El-sayed For Gop Rival In All-important Battleground State

"He stayed on message, pivoting to affordability both times he was asked. That's real discipline. But when you listen to the full episode, he never uses the word racist. He questions why the topic keeps coming up and ties it to his name and his faith. He's pointing to bias.

"If El-Sayed were my client, I'd advise him to name the bias claim directly instead of leaving it implied, then answer the follow-up on what his position actually means in the same breath. Right now, the framing comes first, and he still hasn't answered the follow-up."

title: What a Nile crocodile case means for Trump’s DC building projects
description: The Supreme Court’s 5-4 decision backing President Donald Trump’s massive ballroom at the White House is already playing into challenges over his other pet projects and has renewed a debate over a leg...
fullText:
The Supreme Court's 5-4 decision backing President Donald Trump's massive ballroom at the White House is already playing into challenges over his other pet projects and has renewed a debate over a legal doctrine tied to an abandoned California ski resort and crocodiles in Egypt.

Over the objection of Chief Justice John Roberts and the court's three liberals, five conservative justices last week barred a historic preservationist from suing over the $400 million ballroom for "aesthetic" reasons. The Trump administration has rushed to use that decision to shut down lawsuits against the president's other construction plans for the nation's capital.

At the heart of some of those cases are questions about the scope of "aesthetic standing," or the idea that Americans have a right to sue in some instances based on changes that deprive them of the enjoyment of seeing a landscape, for instance, or an endangered animal.

Trump argues that critics suing over his projects have not met that seemingly subjective standard. And when it came to his ballroom on the White House grounds, five justices agreed.

"This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before," the court wrote Monday in a 5-4, unsigned decision, which allowed Trump to continue work that is already well underway. "We have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury."

In the days since, the Justice Department quickly inserted that Supreme Court order into lower courts reviewing the president's 250-foot arch proposed on a bank of the Potomac River and an effort to remodel a public golf course in Washington, DC.

Other cases, such as the administration's beleaguered effort to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and to paint an iconic Gilded Age government building near the White House, have also raised questions about standing. On Friday, federal court reviewing the Reflecting Pool case ordered a new round of briefing in light of the ballroom ruling.

The challenge with aesthetic standing, said Robert Pushaw, a professor at Pepperdine University Caruso School of Law, is that "aesthetic injury is a gut call." That's because, he said, aesthetics are a matter of personal taste and inherently subjective.

Because it came in an emergency docket case, the court's decision Monday technically has limited precedential value.

"But the case does indicate where five conservative justices are going, and they might be inclined in a later case to either reject aesthetic injuries or limit them to plaintiffs challenging environmental laws," Pushaw said. "Either way, however, plaintiffs suing over alleged legal violations will have great difficulty establishing standing."

Around the same time the Supreme Court was tightening standing rules for federal courts in the 1970s, the justices introduced the idea of aesthetic standing in a case challenging a Disney ski resort in Sequoia National Park.

In that case, Sierra Club v. Morton, Justice Potter Stewart wrote that "aesthetic and environmental wellbeing" are "important ingredients of the quality of life" and are not less deserving of legal protection than "economic wellbeing."

The plaintiff in that case, the court ruled, ultimately did not have standing to sue. (The ski resort was nevertheless later abandoned.)

In his dissent Monday, Roberts also cited a 1992 decision challenging foreign aid for a project that wildlife groups feared would affect the habitat of the endangered Nile crocodile.

In that case, a 6-3 court concluded the plaintiffs did not have standing to sue, but not before the court wrote that "of course" the desire to "use or observe an animal species, even for purely esthetic purposes" is "undeniably a cognizable interest for purpose of standing."

With the court's rejection of the ballroom lawsuit Roberts wrote, "it now is the case that 'I want to look at a crocodile' can adequately answer the ever critical 'what's it to you?' question" of standing, but that "'I want to look at the White House' cannot."

If the historic preservation groups and their members don't have standing to sue, it's not clear who does and whether Trump's projects can be stopped by federal courts.

But groups and experts who have closely followed the growing disputes over Trump's projects say there remains plenty of room for those challenges to continue despite the high court's ballroom decision.

Nicolas Sansone with the Public Citizen Litigation Group, and the lead attorney challenging the arch, told CNN the case is different.

"Irrespective of how we view that analysis on its own terms, we believe that our case presents meaningfully different facts and we're prepared to explain those factual distinctions to a district court," he said in an interview before the administration announced its plans to break ground on the arch.

Sara Bronin, a George Washington University law professor who served as chair of the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation during President Joe Biden's administration, said the court's decision in the ballroom case "makes it harder, but not impossible, for preservationists to use litigation to force the federal government to follow its own rules to protect historic places."

Plaintiffs challenging those projects, she said, "will just need to more fully articulate the ways the challenged action harms or will harm them."

Trump and his supporters have argued the theory of standing raised by the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the ballroom case would have allowed virtually anyone to stop a government building project just because they didn't like the design.

"The National Trust for Historic Preservation artificially created standing from one member's opinion who said the completed building would diminish her personal enjoyment of visiting the White House," Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, a Republican, told CNN.

"Activists cannot be allowed to manufacture standing from personal displeasure and use it to stop any project they oppose," he said.

Trump has repeatedly said the same, in coarser language, all year.

"There is absolutely no argument that a woman walking her dog in the vicinity of the White House has STANDING to stop such a desperately needed National Security structure for the people of the United States of America, as it will provide Presidents, current and future, a secure space to do their jobs, especially when she never saw the Building, because it had not risen, and she had no rendering, or pictures of the Building because they, also, were in the formative stages of production," the president wrote in a Truth Social post last month.

CNN's Sunlen Serfaty and Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

title: US ambassador to Israel says there is no plan to force Palestinians out of Gaza
description: TURMUS AYYA, West Bank, Sept 4 (Reuters) - U.S.
fullText:
TURMUS AYYA, West Bank, Sept 4 (Reuters) - U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Saturday ‌said there was no plan to force ‌Palestinians to leave Gaza after two Israeli ministers this week floated ​proposals for the mass removal of Palestinians from the coastal territory.

• "I can tell you categorically there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people ‌out of Gaza against ⁠their will," Huckabee told reporters in Turmus Ayya, a Palestinian town in the ⁠Israeli-occupied West Bank.

• "There is an open-mindedness (that) if people wish to leave that they should have the right ​to leave. ​To incarcerate them in ​a place they don't ‌want to be should be an absolute, I think, just disgrace," Huckabee said.

• "Nobody is suggesting that there will be forced displacement. The Israelis are not. The Americans are certainly not. I know of ‌no one who supports that."

• ​Defence Minister Israel Katz on ​Wednesday said there ​was "no real solution for Gaza in the ‌end without this migration."

• Far-right ​security minister ​Itamar Ben-Gvir on Thursday outlined a seven-year plan for removing Gaza's population through what he ​described as "voluntary emigration."

• ‌Israel is to hold a general election ​on October 27.

title: Barry Morphew arrested days after being ordered on house arrest for alleged hit-and-run
description: Murder suspect Barry Morphew was arrested on Thursday in Boulder, Colorado, authorities said, days after his alleged involvement in a hit-and-run crash on August 26 in Denver, court records show.
fullText:
Murder suspect Barry Morphew was arrested on Thursday in Boulder, Colorado, authorities said, days after his alleged involvement in a hit-and-run crash on August 26 in Denver, court records show.

A "concerned citizen" saw Morphew, 58, drive "aggressively prior to striking two vehicles," Alamosa County District Judge Amanda Hopkins wrote in a court order.

One of the drivers took video of the interaction, Hopkins said, adding she viewed part of the video that was included in a news report from CNN affiliate KCNC.

"During the interaction, a person who is very clearly the Defendant refused to provide his name or identification and indicated … he does not have insurance. The Defendant offered the other driver $300 for the damage to her vehicle, which she refused, and he is seen buffing the scratches on the other driver's vehicle with his hand and tshirt," Hopkins wrote in the order.

The defendant fled, "almost striking another individual and driving over a curb to do so," after the other driver rejected the cash offer and said she was calling police, according to the court order.

Morphew, who was out on $3 million bond after he was re-arrested last year on a first-degree murder charge in connection with the death of his wife, Suzanne Morphew, allegedly violated the terms of his release, the judge's order said.

Morphew's release terms generally confine him to his home, "except for medical appointments or emergencies, to meet with his legal team or attend court, or to work," the court order states.

Christina, who was in one of the cars that were hit, recorded video of the incident in which she repeatedly asks Morphew for his insurance and ID, and he attempts to rub off the scratches on her car. The woman spoke on the condition that CNN would not use her surname.

As Morphew then begins to flee, the driver of the other car can be seen standing in front of his vehicle, apparently trying to block him from driving away, video shows. Morphew then maneuvers the car in reverse and drives away from the scene.

Christina said she did not recognize Morphew, but her mom recognized him in the video when she watched it the next day.

GPS data requested by the 12th Judicial District Attorney's Office showed Morphew left home and drove to Denver International Airport where it was "possible he was picking up his daughter," his attorneys told the district attorney's office.

Going to the airport for any purpose other than work "constitutes a breach of his bond" and "also presents an extreme flight risk," the district attorney's office wrote in a court filing asking the judge to modify Morphew's bond.

Morphew drove "in areas of hotels and a mall at various points in the day," before GPS data pinpoints him "in the area of the alleged crash" in Denver, court documents show.

On Wednesday, Hopkins issued an order for Morphew to "remain in his home at all times, no exceptions." Boulder County deputies arrested Morphew Thursday night for failing to comply with the order, according to the Boulder County Sheriff's Office.

Morphew has not been charged in connection with the Denver hit-and-run, KCNC said.

He was booked into the Boulder County Jail, the sheriff's office said, and a court filing shows he has a bond hearing scheduled on Tuesday.

Morphew had been released on bond after his arrest in relation to the murder allegation because Colorado law at the time only allowed defendants to be held without bail in "certain, extremely limited, circumstances" that did not apply to him, according to the judge.

Voters have since expanded the circumstances under which defendants can be denied bail, but the change is unlikely to apply to Morphew because he was charged before it took effect, according to court documents.

CNN contacted Morphew's attorneys for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Suzanne Morphew, 49, vanished while on a Mother's Day bike ride in 2020 near Maysville, Colorado, about 110 miles away from Colorado Springs.

Barry Morphew was first charged with murder in connection with her disappearance in May 2021, but prosecutors dropped the case, saying they wanted more time to find Suzanne's body.

Because the initial charges against Morphew were dismissed without prejudice, prosecutors could pursue a case against him later.

In 2023, the mother-of-two's remains were found 50 miles away from where she was reported missing.

A 2024 autopsy report released by the El Paso County coroner said Suzanne Morphew's death was a "homicide by unspecified means in the setting of butorphanol, azaperone, and medetomidine intoxication."

The combination of the three drugs is often used to immobilize wildlife and can cause analgesia and sedation, the coroner's office said.

A tranquilizer gun and accessories were found in the Morphews' home, according to investigators.

Barry Morphew was arrested in Arizona after a Colorado grand jury returned an indictment in June 2025.

Morphew has maintained his innocence since his wife disappeared. He has pleaded not guilty and faces trial next summer in the death of his wife, according to The Associated Press.

CNN's Taylor Galgano, Emma Tucker and Yan Kaner contributed to this report.

title: Democratic lawmakers erupt after anti-Israel journalist calls Hakeem Jeffries an ‘AIPAC monkey’ in viral rant
description: Rula Jebreal's "AIPAC monkey" remark about Hakeem Jeffries sparked swift backlash from the Congressional Black Caucus and Democratic lawmakers.
fullText:
Anti-Israel journalist Rula Jebreal apologized "unconditionally" after calling House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., an "AIPAC monkey" during an interview earlier this week, a remark the Congressional Black Caucus and several Democratic lawmakers condemned as blatantly racist.

The comment came as Jebreal appeared on Wajahat Ali's "The Left Hook" podcast Wednesday and accused Jeffries, who is Black, of carrying out the agenda of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and blasted his support for Israel.

"His name is Hakeem. 'Hakeem' is an Arabic name which means 'healer.' He's not a healer, he's a divider," Jebreal said.

Left-wing Podcaster Blasts Schumer, Jeffries As 'Fascist Collaborators'

"He is a bought and paid by AIPAC monkey," she added. "With all due respect — and I don't mean it in a racist way." Jebreal continued, "He is just basically an errand boy, and we're done and tired."

Immediately following Jebreal's comments, host Ali sought to clarify the meaning behind her remarks.

"I know you corrected yourself, Rula, but I just want to address it," Ali said. "Using monkey to anyone Black, it has terrible racial connotations. But I think you caught yourself and said you didn't mean it with any racial animosity."

"I didn't," Jebreal replied. "There's these three monkeys — one, I cannot hear, I cannot see, I cannot speak. It reminds me of these three monkeys."

However, the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) rejected Jebreal's explanation of her controversial comments, with other Democratic leaders following suit.

"To be clear, there isn't a non-racist way to call Leader Jeffries — a Black man — a 'monkey' or 'errand boy,'" the group said in a statement posted to X.

Some Democrats Privately Disgusted By Hasan Piker But Are Afraid To Publicly Criticize Him, House Dem Claims

The CBC then pointed to Ali, the podcast's host and a staunch critic of Israel, adding, "This is what happens when we hold ourselves to such low standards for what's allowable in our discourse — people get comfortable being openly bigoted."

"We have to stop platforming and trafficking in anti-Black racism, whether it's on the political right or the left."

Dem Senate Candidate Makes Stunning Admission About Antisemitism In Her Party: 'Dangerous'

Her comments also drew criticism from several Democratic lawmakers, who took to X to condemn the inflammatory statement.

"Blatantly racist and offensive rhetoric — it should be condemned by everyone, across the political spectrum. Period," Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., posted online.

Democrats Condemning Hasan Piker As Backlash Spreads Through Party

Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y., echoed the same sentiment, posting, "Calling a Black man a 'monkey' is racist. Full stop.

"If Wajahat Ali and Rula Jebreal were on the far right, no one on the far left would have any trouble condemning them for dehumanizing a Black man in racist terms," he continued. "The silence is deafening."

Democrat Rips Hasan Piker As 'Hack Who Thrives On Hate' Over His Warning To American Jews About Israel

After the clip circulated online, Jebreal posted an apology to X.

"I am disgusted and horrified that Hakeem Jeffries is taking money from AIPAC amidst Israel's genocide in Palestine," Jebreal wrote. "That said, a term that I used to describe him was inappropriate and offensive and should never have been used. I apologize unconditionally."

However, Jebreal's attempts at damage control drew a skeptical read from Axia Public Relations CEO Jason Mudd.

"She reasserts the accusation first and tucks the apology at the end. That's not confessing. That's a closing argument with 'sorry' bolted on," Mudd told Fox News Digital.

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

"The podcast clarification and the written apology target two different audiences: One tried to survive the moment live, the other tried to survive the headline."

Jebreal and Jeffries did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Iran to tackle economic issues, says further attacks will be 'more painful'
description: DUBAI, Sept 6 () - Iran said it will step up efforts to tackle problems created by the U. sanctions that are crippling its economy, while a senior Iranian official warned of a "painful response" if it...
fullText:
DUBAI, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Iran said it will step up efforts to tackle problems created by the U.S. sanctions that are crippling its economy, while a senior Iranian official warned of a "painful response" if it comes under further attack.

Six months after U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran, the war appears to be at a stalemate. A preliminary ceasefire accord ‌reached in June has unravelled and little progress has been made in diplomatic efforts to get the peace process back on track.

After a pause in military action for much of ‌August, tit-for-tat strikes have resumed with U.S. Central Command saying it hit three Iranian tankers on Saturday after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships.

Following the attacks, Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Sunday that the ​U.S. should understand that the rules of the game in the war against Iran have changed "before it is too late".

"From now on, any attack against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response," he said in a speech published on his Telegram channel.

Tehran has shown it retains the capability to attack U.S. interests in neighbouring countries and to shut down oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil supplies flowed prior to the conflict.

SANCTIONS, OIL BLOCKADE SQUEEZE ECONOMY

However, the U.S. campaign to throttle Iran's economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult ‌to withstand, three senior Iranian sources have said.

In his speech on Sunday, ⁠Qalibaf added that alongside the military front, Iran's main battle was now over production and people's livelihoods.

He cited sharp currency fluctuations, inflation, unemployment and market management as major challenges, adding Iranians could tolerate hardship but not mismanagement or inaction and expected the government to act quickly.

Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said that Tehran planned ⁠to respond to U.S. economic pressure with reforms and rejected the notion that sanctions would cause it to change course, according to state media on Sunday.

"They speak of economic pressure and isolation, of breaking off financial ties and they think that by pressuring the economy of a country they can change the decisions of its people," Madanizadeh said.

"I have to clarify one point: the responsibility of reforming Iran's economy is with its government and people, not ​with ​the U.S. Treasury."

Separately, Economy Ministry deputy Morteza Zamanian said on Sunday that the ministry's "Economic War Headquarters" was doubling down ​on its work to resolve problems caused by the war, according to the semi-official ‌Tasnim news agency.

KHARG ISLAND HIT 550 TIMES IN PRIOR MONTHS, IRAN SAYS

Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90% of its crude via its Kharg Island export hub before the war. Flows have been disrupted since a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.

On Sunday, U.S. Central Command said on X that as of September 6 it had redirected 92 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two to ensure strict compliance with its blockade.

On August 31, Trump issued a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video depicting Kharg Island being "blown to smithereens." Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.

In an interview aired on state TV on Sunday, Iran's Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad said the island had been hit around 550 times in previous months ‌but continued to operate.

Iran has also imposed a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, creating an issue for U.S. ​President Donald Trump by pushing up fuel prices globally ahead of midterm elections for his Republican Party in November.

However, U.S. ​Energy Secretary Chris Wright said oil was getting through the waterway.

"Our transits through the Strait are ​averaging over 9 million barrels a day now, and with the access pipelines that go around the Strait, we're probably two thirds or more of pre-conflict flows. ‌So Iranians are still causing trouble, but the United States Navy is winning ​that battle," he told CNN.

On Saturday, U.S. Central Command ​said it struck three Iranian vessels, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships.

The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against U.S. military vessels in the region, and said later it targeted the three tankers as well as three U.S.-linked vessels in other areas.

Tasnim, the semi-official Iranian news agency, had reported that ​four U.S. missiles hit a tanker in the area of Kharg's anchorage. ‌Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker's crew was being evacuated.

No American personnel were harmed, Central Command said.

On Sunday, Tasnim reported that the ​IRGC had shot down a U.S. surveillance balloon over Erbil in northern Iraq, describing it as part of a broader effort to eliminate U.S. aerial surveillance and early-warning systems ​in the region.

title: Baby girl dies while camping with family in woods
description: A police cordon remains in place at a wooded area near to Strawberry Lane in Cheslyn Hay.
fullText:
A three-month-old girl has died while camping in woodland with her family, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to land off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at 08:45 BST on Saturday, to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

"While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident," Det Insp Katie Gregory said. "The death is being treated as unexplained at this time."

People living in the close-knit community, a village of around 7,000 people, have been left shocked by the child's death.

The area is not an official camping site but locals said teenagers would often fish in two pools there and camp overnight.

The nature trail is also popular with dog walkers and runners.

A police cordon remained in place in the woodland on Sunday, and officers were in the area carrying out inquiries and providing reassurance.

A bunch of roses was also left nearby, in tribute to the little girl.

Councillor Robert Duncan said the community was devastated. He also urged residents to "avoid speculation and allow the family and responders the privacy and respect they deserve".

The scene of the tragedy was described as "hidden away" from the main woodland in the Wyrley and Essington Branch Canal Local Nature Reserve.

The cordon surrounds the scene, which is close to the fishing lake, and two camping tents - one of which is white with a navy blue trim - have been pitched.

Hundreds of residents have paid tribute on social media, with one saying: "Heartbreaking news, our thoughts and prayers are with family and friends at this very sad time."

"May it bring a tiny bit of comfort in knowing villagers care and are saddened by the news."

The Superintendent of the Cannock Chase Methodist Church Circuit, Rev Samantha Hagerman, said: "Our thoughts and prayers are with family, friends and emergency services affected by the incident near Cheslyn Hay yesterday."

Follow BBC Stoke & Staffordshire on BBC Sounds, Facebook, X and Instagram.

title: Trump’s ‘dumb’ story makes no sense
description: There are far more important issues to discuss. But in these divided times, surely we can all come together for a brief moment and agree that President Donald Trump’s “dumb” story makes no sense.
fullText:
There are far more important issues to discuss. But in these divided times, surely we can all come together for a brief moment and agree that President Donald Trump's "dumb" story makes no sense.

Trump has been saying it over and over for months, straight-faced and dead serious, as he tries to brand Democrats as "Dumocrats." The president who has a long history of asserting nobody knew things lots of people actually knew is this time declaring that…nobody knows, or at least most people don't know, that "dumb" ends with the letter B.

"Most people don't know that 'dumb' has a B at the end," he told Republican lawmakers at the White House on Wednesday. "You know, they think it's D-U-M, and that's okay."

"Most people don't know that 'dumb' has a B," he said at the White House Correspondents' Dinner in July.

"Nobody knows that 'dumb' has a B," he said in a New York Post interview in June.

"Most people don't know that, you know, 'dumb' ends with a B. But most people don't know," he said in a Fox News interview in May.

To be very generous to Trump, his "most people" claim cannot be authoritatively fact-checked because there has not been a national spelling test on the word "dumb." And it's certainly true that some Americans struggle with literacy in general and spelling in particular.

But…come on here. "Dumb"? A common four-letter word kids learn in grade school? Most people know how to spell "dumb." This is obvious.

So why is the president of the United States going out of his way to establish a fantasy world in which most people don't know – or even that nobody knows – a thing most people clearly know?

We don't believe the critics who claim it's because Trump himself just learned "dumb" has a B. Rather, it's more likely this nonsense is a product of the president's insistence on being constantly and universally viewed as brilliant – that someone questioned the wisdom of "Dumocrat," his preferred spelling of the juvenile insult, and he preferred to justify it by making the public sound woefully ignorant rather than admit this might not be his finest nicknaming work.

"If you replace the E with a U, instead of Democrat you have Dumocrat," the president explained on Tuesday, as he has on multiple previous occasions. "And most people don't know that 'dumb' has a B at the end. You know, they think it's D-U-M, and that's okay. So it's a one-letter change and you go no more E, you just put a D, and you got a Dumocrat."

We'll never know for certain what is happening here. Which is fine given how dumb this whole thing is.

title: Titans' Tony Pollard got extra motivation during the offseason
description: Tennessee Titans' Tony Pollard feels like an underdog after offseason chatter and is motivated to prove himself in 2026.
fullText:
For most of the offseason, the Tennessee Titans' focus has been on building around quarterback Cam Ward.

Everything from head coach Robert Saleh hiring Brian Daboll as offensive coordinator to bringing in Wan'Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate was made to help Ward develop in year two. But one weapon who can be an asset to Ward in 2026 often gets overlooked: Tony Pollard.

In fact, in April, a large portion of the fanbase was ready to move on from Pollard, calling on the organization to draft Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love. While the Arizona Cardinals eventually prevented that from happening, Pollard told Tyler Dunne of Go Long that he got the message loud and clear and now has something to prove in what could be his final season in Nashville.

"It all put me back into the prime spot to feel like I'm the underdog," Pollard says. "I'm easily overlooked. So it's easy for me to get up and get going. It's easy for me to grind and give my all every day because I know they might not be expecting that from me, or they may be surprised by the things that I'm doing. I look at it as motivation."

Pollard ran hard in training camp and looked the part of the Titans' feature back behind an offensive line that looked good as run blockers. If he can continue to build upon that once the season starts, his emergence could set the Titans' offense for success, and who knows, maybe a couple more seasons in Nashville.

title: How Tennessee football's Mike Matthews is setting stage for return home
description: Wide receiver Mike Matthews set personal highs with 132 yards and two touchdowns from Faizon Brandon in Tennessee football's season opener.
fullText:
Mike Matthews opened the 2026 season for Tennessee football with a bang, setting personal single-game highs with 132 receiving yards and two touchdowns in the 56-9 win over Furman at Neyland Stadium on Sept. 5.

The outing has the junior wide receiver soaring into Week 2, when the No. 18 Vols (1-0) play Georgia Tech (0-1) at Bobby Dodd Stadium in Atlanta, just 22 miles from his hometown of Lilburn.

"It's a pretty good confidence-builder, but I've been working hard all offseason," Matthews said. "I kind of knew that my heart is going to show when I play on the field, so I try to play with heart. God put me in a good position and it played out the right way."

Matthews enjoyed a breakout season for the Vols in 2025, setting career highs for receptions (32), yards (813) and touchdowns (four). Entering 2026, he's catching passes from his third different starting quarterback in as many years.

It was the first game he played with five-star freshman quarterback Faizon Brandon, but they clearly have developed a quick and easy connection.

Matthews' two touchdown receptions went for 55 and 57 yards. The first came on a busted coverage from Furman, when Brandon's running ability drew a safety up enough for Matthews to run free behind the defense. Matthews had to fight through contact to haul in the second score.

"It was just like practice," Matthews said. "A lot of our deep balls have just been on point every time, so it was nothing I wasn't used to."

Matthews was happy about the win to start the season, but immediately after beating Furman, his attention turned to Georgia Tech.

"It just fills me up, makes me proud," he said about playing close to home. "But coming up, I know I got to lock in for next week, get ready for the game, prepare and just be who I am."

title: Refs, Bryce Underwood big losers in Michigan's miracle win vs WMU
description: Andrew Birkle picks the winners and losers from Michigan football's shocking Week 1 13-12 win over Western Michigan on a Hail Mary in Ann Arbor.
fullText:
Free Press sports writer Andrew Birkle picks the winners and losers from Michigan football's shocking Week 1 13-12 win over Western Michigan on a Hail Mary in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Sept. 5, in Kyle Whittingham's first game as Michigan's coach.

How about a memory-making miracle in your first game in maize and blue?

Just absurd stuff from Buchanan, a Utah transfer touted as a big-time playmaker by Michigan's new staff, and showed what he has in his bag by hauling in Michigan's second Hail Mary attempt, after a controversial decision by the refs to save Michigan.

He finished with just six catches but gained 126 yards, boosted by his 47-yard touchdown catch with no time on the clock.

NO JOY IN ANN ARBOR? Hail Mary fuels conspiracists as Michigan football pays for its past

JJ Buchanan with a beautiful one-handed snag 👏 @UMichFootball

📺: NBC pic.twitter.com/YNyKCElan4

Michigan's defensive end factory continues to produce winners.

Nichols looks like the next productive edge rusher for the Wolverines after Derrick Moore and Jaishawn Barham departed for the NFL draft.

On Western's second drive, Nichols made a nice tackle to stuff a Broncos run, then sacked quarterback Broc Lowry to force a punt.

SHAWN WINDSOR: Michigan football had every reason to lose to WMU. But history had other ideas

That was just one sequence in a dominant first half that included five total tackles, 1½ sacks and 2½ tackles for loss.

He finished the day with nine total tackles and it looks like Michigan's got another dude on the defensive line to pair with 2025 All-American John Henry Daley when he gets more healthy.

This one will be discussed for years to come, and rightfully so.

There were literally zeroes on the clock. Michigan was the loser, Western Michigan the winner in Ann Arbor.

When the refs announced a review, it seemed like a formality. However, after a lengthy holdup, referee Jim Wharrie's crew announced – without much explanation – that there was 1 second on the clock, seemingly because the WMU defender touched the ball while out of bounds.

TV TIME: Michigan football Hail Mary winner questioned as time appeared to run out

However, NBC rules analyst Terry McAauley vehemently disagreed with the crew's decision:

"Our in-set clock is in-synch, is the actual stadium clock, the ball isn't even close to touching a player when it goes to zero," McAauley said on the NBC broadcast. "Now their system, their Hawk-eye system, apparently either had a different synch or whatever and they came up with 1 second when it touched the players. I don't see how that happened, assuming our clock is correct.

"It is clearly not touching a player, the ball is clearly still in the air when the clock goes to zero, on our screens. The Big Ten is going to have to tell a lot of us how did they get to one second on this play."

McAauley's reaction lines up with the eye test. Assuming there's not another angle, this could be an all-time blunder and one that potentially stole history from Western Michigan.

There were plenty of excuses to be made for Underwood after his first season in Ann Arbor: no designated quarterback coach, getting flung into a messy coaching situation, unrealistic expectations – and the Wolverines still went 9-4. The hope was that an offseason working under new offensive coordinator Jason Beck would correct many of the mechanical and processing issues Underwood showed as a freshman.

Outside of an impressive first drive in which he went 5-for-5 for 61 yards, another 11 yards rushing and a TD on the ground, things went about as bad as possible for Underwood.

After leading an 11-play, 75-yard drive that was capped off with a QB sneak from Underwood, Michigan went punt, punt, punt, punt, interception. And that included some lucky breaks. On Michigan's second drive, Underwood tried to play hero and squeeze in a pass down the sideline on third and long and was intercepted before it was ruled Western's defender tipped the ball while a few inches out of bounds, negating the pick. On the last drive before the half, Underwood recklessly threw a pass in the boundary that was well-read and intercepted by linebacker Dillon Moore; it easily could've been a pick-six if Moore's momentum hadn't landed him on the sideline at the 26.

As if things could get worse, Underwood barely got the ball in the second half with Western's dominant ball control, and when he did have it, things went terribly.

Michigan opened the half with two punts and then Underwood had a crushing fumble to give WMU the ball back deep in Michigan territory.

A Hail Mary connection will certainly buy him some good will, but before that, he was just 10-for-15 passing for just 95 yards with nine carries for 47 yards rushing.

There's still a lot of work to be done.

REACTIONS: Michigan fans get second lease on life after Hail Mary: 'Man I love football'

If I had to sum up this insane game for Michigan ... well, I can't really use the words in a family publication that come to mind for the plays between the first and final drives.

Michigan's first drive of the game couldn't have gone better, ending in a touchdown after 11 plays. Michigan didn't score again until the last play of the game.

Michigan committed nine penalties for 80 yards.

Michigan's offensive line was pushed around all game, forcing Underwood to play under pressure and creating no gaps for a run game that picked up just 106 yards on the ground.

Underwood reverted back to so many of the old bad habits that Michigan fans were hoping that Beck and Co. spent the offseason fixing.

Michigan's defense, which was far from the biggest problem, allowed a 20-play drive that milked nearly 14 minutes off the clock and tilted the game heavily in Western's favor.

In Nick Saban's first year at Alabama, the Crimson Tide lost to University of Louisiana-Monroe.

Whittingham and Beck were saved from a loss on that level of ignominy with a miracle catch by Buchanan, but this was far from the ideal start for Michigan, which has a lot to fix before Oklahoma comes to town next week.

One of the most frequent topics this summer on "Hail Yes!", the Free Press' Michigan football and basketball podcast, was if Marsh could be the person to break Michigan's 1,000-yard receiver drought.

The wideout was unbelievable in the second half of the season last year, finishing with 651 yards and five total touchdowns after having just one catch in the first four games.

This did not look like the start to a breakout year.

Marsh muffed a punt in the first quarter that led to a WMU field goal and finished with just two catches for 17 yards before garbage time. This game won't be remembered for Marsh's poor performance, but he left a lot to be desired.

Andrew Birkle is an assistant sports editor for the Free Press. Contact him via email at abirkle@freepress.com.

title: Social media reacts to Nebraska's win over the Ohio Bobcats
description: Social media was buzzing after the Huskers defeated the Bobcats on Saturday afternoon.
fullText:
Nebraska football defeated the Ohio Bobcats 49-21 on Saturday. It was a tense few moments for Husker fans, as Nebraska led only 14-13 at halftime.

Nevertheless, Nebraska used a solid fourth quarter to pull away in the end. They scored 21 total points in the fourth quarter alone, giving them their first win of the season.

Freshman running back Jamal Rule made his presence felt in this game, as he had 122 rushing yards on 15 carries and two touchdowns. His 100-yard rushing game was the first by a freshman in a season opener since quarterback Adrian Martinez had 117 rushing yards against Colorado in the 2018 opener

Quarterback Anthony Colandrea completed 18-of-32 passes for 275 yards and three touchdowns in his Nebraska debut. Nebraska also had eight pass breakups in the game, its most since 2024.

Nebraska's victory marked the third straight year it has won its season opener and was the 100th victory in a season opener in program history. The Huskers are 100-32-5 all-time in season openers.

Overall, it was not a complete game, but the Huskers managed to put things together in the second half to get the job done. Social media reacted strongly to the victory, as the Huskers look ahead to Bowling Green.
